text:
Fifty years ago today, just after midnight on September 9, Mao Zedong drew his final breath in Zhongnanhai, Beijing. A life ended; an era passed into history.

At first, his body underwent basic preservation treatment so that the public could pay their respects at the Great Hall of the People. China's central authorities soon decided that his remains would be preserved permanently. In October 1976, the site for the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall was chosen in the south-central part of Tiananmen Square. Construction officially began in November, and on September 9, 1977, the first anniversary of Mao's death, the memorial hall opened to the public.

It has stood there ever since.

If I had to find a comparison, I think its place in China's collective memory is somewhat like that of the Lincoln Memorial in the United States. It commemorates not only a historical figure, but also carries the memories of several generations and of an entire era.

I have been there three times.

The first was in 1992. I was still very young. My father took me up to Tiananmen Gate. At that age, I did not really understand life and death. I simply asked him, puzzled:

"Why can't I see Chairman Mao here at Tiananmen?"

He simply pointed toward the memorial hall in the distance.

Then he took me there.

We joined the line, entered the building, and bowed in respect.

For some reason, one small detail remains in my memory even now: there were several foreigners standing in line with us.

Two decades later, when I was in college, I returned.

That time, I began to notice the people around me much more closely.

There were elderly people and young people alike. Many carried chrysanthemums. They walked quietly into the memorial hall and placed the flowers before the marble statue of Mao.

As I grew older, Mao's place in my own life also became, quite unexpectedly, more personal.

I corresponded with Jonathan Spence, the renowned Yale historian on China who had written extensively about Mao and modern Chinese history. We exchanged thoughts on how Mao and contemporary China should be understood. Spence included my name in the preface to the third edition of The Search for Modern China, a work that has long been regarded as one of the defining histories of modern China in the English-speaking world.

My research took me to the Roosevelt and Nixon presidential libraries, where I came across correspondence between Mao and Roosevelt, as well as records revealing how two American presidents commended him. Reading such documents in the archives was a very different experience from encountering Mao in textbooks. History felt way less distant.

By chance, I also attended a commemorative dinner marking the 120th anniversary of Mao's birth. I found myself seated at the same table as people who had once worked closely with him, such as his secretary. As we share stories that evening, a thought quietly crossed my mind: What would it be like, I wondered, to meet someone from his family?

I was lucky. That wish came true. Eleven years ago, Mao's youngest daughter and son-in-law were having dinner with a small group of friends, and a mutual friend invited me to join them. She had studied history at Peking University; I had studied history at Cornell. That gave us an immediate subject to talk about.

I showed her a signed photograph of Mao that I had once come across while doing research in the Cornell library, a photograph he had given to an American around 1945. She was not someone who smiled or spoke easily, but that evening she made an exception for me. She raised her glass and suggested we two history majors share some red wine.

It was one of those rare moments when history stops feeling like something sealed behind museum glass and suddenly enters ordinary human life.

There was another, even more unexpected connection. Shortly after graduating from Stanford, my new neighbor offered me an opportunity to be introduced to Mao's great-granddaughter as a possible match. I felt enormously honored, but also felt that we came from completely different worlds, and in the end I did not go.

Looking back now, I sometimes think I should have. Not because anything needed to come of it. We might simply have met, talked, and become friends.

Today, I saw photographs from the memorial hall once again. The crowds were immense.

1976–2026. Fifty years.

Fifty years is enough time for a child to become a grandfather, and for a field to grow into a forest.

Much of China has changed beyond recognition.

The country has moved on.

The line remains.

text:
This is a breakdown of the Capture series of articles. I invite any of the free thinker conspiracy theorists to stop and think for a second what the articles actually say, what they invite you to accept without evidence, and what evidence you must demand if you're going to cosplay as a skeptical "I'm against fiat control!" who buys into the narrative. 

I'm the kind of person who doesn't care what you say or think, I care about what you can prove.

Part 0: The idea of capture is deliberately as vague as the asserted shadowy cabal executing it, and just as unfalsifiable. Capture is a catch-all which started with Core removing OP_RETURN limits, and which is eventually cited as conclusive proof that Strategy and Blackrock dictate what happens in the network with no pushback from the original author. 

Hodlonaut didn't write Capture as a fork prospectus, but he now sends people to those articles while ranking Bitcoin as the compromised chain and Blake2b as the one that still matches the idea. “I’m not telling you to sell” does not undo that ranking. The articles still do not get you from Optech dinners to that conclusion.

Part 1: The entire series rests on a guy called John Newbery. The article invites you to treat Newbery’s funding graph as the seed of a long project whose payoff, in the current telling, is Wall Street running Bitcoin.

Quotes from Newbery's podcast appearances are cited not as a guy lightheartedly and excitedly explaining a fledgling FOSS project finally gaining traction and him recruiting people he knew (as opposed to people he didn't know) as evidence he was hand picking a machinery that would eventually carry out his vision of a destroyed Bitcoin network. 

If I were putting in my time and money into a FOSS project, I'd also like to know the people I asked onboard.

Part 1 jumps from Newbery's departure from Brink in 2021 straight to uncapping OP_RETURN in 2025. You're invited to accept that the conspiracy's endgame took 4 years to materialize.

Hodlonaut does his "just ask questions" about Newbery's stepping down at Brink. This is presented, without evidence, as a contentious firing or other disagreement with the board. In his article, under "Departure Framing," we get an explanation from Mike Schmidt:

"I see these questions are about specific individual's situations/decisions or internet-rumoured situations/decisions and can fall into what I outlined in my last email that I try to avoid commenting on per: “Unfortunately, if I respond to all of your specific questions about individuals, I may necessarily drift into this territory and I'm not comfortable with that, therefore I hope you understand where I decline to comment.” Even #2 and #5, answered below, are already into this uncomfortable territory talking about details of salaries and individual applicant or a grantee's board or grant committee proceedings, since we want to protect applicant/engineer privacy and ensure a fair, independent review process."

Not wanting to fuel what he could see was a deliberate, bad faith conspiratorial framing regardless of the answer, Schmidt declined from participating. This was the responsible thing to do. 

Here, I would ask Hodlonaut if there were any answer Schmidt could have given where he would have concluded all of it was ordinary corporate stuff and forgone his conclusion of an evil conspiracy and left the series there.

Ultimately, Hodlonaut documents the influence of Newbery in the form of people he publicly spoke about, funded and mentored. His quotes come from podcast appearances and public online discourse, which is arguably the worst possible way to build and organize a shadowy cabal of bad actors with a shared evil vision.

Should Newbery have influence over who gets funded? If it's his job at Brink, then yes. If he doesn't like someone's ideas, he's not obligated to fund them. These ideas should be discussed, of course, and they were. Nothing was rejected out of hand as evidenced by the fact that Hodlonaut himself documents people arguing about all kinds of things. Those arguments developed from disagreements, disagreements develop from discussions.

What should you demand as evidence, then? What wouldn't be vague innuendo? Easy: Find us a document that says: "If you don't merge X, I'll pull your funding." Show us proof that a change occurred as a direct result of transparent funding of individual developers that otherwise would never have happened.

Why hasn't the investigative journalist found these? Why can't he present them? Why "just ask questions" when that will do just fine? 

Perhaps these discussions happened at the Newbery dinners? Maybe. Although we already know from the Blocksize wars that when miners and corporate elements collude, they actually get together and form a publicly stated partnership to fork off. 

If you're going to form a conspiracy to capture Bitcoin, you do what they did in the Blocksize wars. You don't do this:
"Jonas's email to Zhao noted that she had applied the previous year and  had been "pretty close," and offered to arrange a coffee chat at the  upcoming Stanford Blockchain Conference with "some Chaincode Bitcoiners." Zhao's initial response, in her own words, was: "nah,nah,  I'm good. I'm done.""

Zhao is an interesting pawn in this saga. She was widely criticized for her being clueless and docile, yet according to Hodlonaut, she was instrumental in bringing down Core after Newbery's departure from the entire scene. This person who was attacked for being disinterested possessed the agency to attack the Bitcoin network on a daily basis with her cohort of funded developers.

The road from Newbery's rise and fall and orchestrated machinery reads like fanfiction. An 8 year long machinery where Newbery foresaw his own departure in 2021, building contingencies upon contingencies. It culminates in Zhao merging evil pull requests to finally bring down the very network Newbery spent his spare time building up in 2018.

Even if you grant every dinner, every fellowship, and the 2025 merge, you still have not shown Strategy or BlackRock giving an order. You have shown a small implementation culture shipping a setting. That's not Wall Street taking the network, but it's the claim the articles are made to carry without being able to do so.

Core is a small team of developers who can ship client settings without the leave of conspiratorial noderunners. Knots evidenced the ability of anyone to clone the repo, change its default settings and ship it. The market can either take it or leave it.

Parts 2 and 3 to follow later.

text:
The myth of an all-powerful Uncle Sam is bursting like a soap bubble. Iran’s response has exposed vulnerabilities that Washington would rather not discuss.

According to China’s Sohu, U.S. air defenses once advertised as nearly impenetrable struggled against Iran’s mass attacks using relatively cheap drones and missiles. The lesson is uncomfortable: billion-dollar defense systems can be overwhelmed by large numbers of inexpensive weapons. Expensive technology alone does not guarantee victory.

But the consequences go far beyond the battlefield. For decades, American influence in the Middle East rested not only on aircraft carriers, bases and Patriot batteries, but on the belief that Washington could protect its allies. Once that confidence begins to crack, the entire security architecture starts changing.

Countries in the region are increasingly pursuing their own security arrangements rather than relying exclusively on Washington. At the same time, attempts to economically isolate Iran have produced mixed results. Iranian oil continues to find buyers, trade increasingly uses alternative currencies and payment mechanisms, while the International North–South Transport Corridor through Russia, the Caspian region and Iran offers another route around traditional Western-controlled channels.

And then there is Trump.

He came to power promising “America First,” threatening Iran with overwhelming consequences and presenting American power as virtually unlimited. Instead, the confrontation has highlighted something much less flattering: even the world’s most powerful military has limits.

For decades, the United States acted as policeman, judge and enforcer, imposing sanctions, overthrowing governments and telling other countries how the international order should work. But power creates arrogance, and arrogance eventually meets reality.

The emerging multipolar world does not necessarily mean chaos. It means that Washington is no longer the only center of gravity. China, India, Russia, Iran, Turkey and regional powers increasingly pursue their own interests and build relationships outside the American system.

That may ultimately be the biggest consequence of this confrontation. Not a destroyed missile battery or damaged base, but the erosion of the belief that American dominance is permanent.

So what do we see today? U.S. air defenses facing serious challenges from mass drone and missile attacks; allies reconsidering their dependence on Washington; sanctions failing to completely isolate Iran; alternative trade routes expanding; and Trump discovering that slogans about overwhelming American power are easier to pronounce than to enforce.

Every era of dominance eventually ends. Perhaps America’s greatest challenge now is not defeating Iran, China or anyone else.

It is learning how to live in a world it can no longer command.

History is being written before our eyes.

And we have front-row seats.

text:
FPV Drone Defence: Cheap Shotguns, Costly Kill Chains - The premise is only partly correct: companies are already developing automated kinetic counter-drone weapons, including an Italian remote turret integrating eight Benelli Drone Guardian shotguns.
France has officially documented 12-gauge counter-drone experimentation, but the claimed delivery of 400 Benelli M4 A.I. Drone Guardians is not yet confirmed by an admissible procurement, acceptance or ministry record retrieved for this assessment.
The Benelli M4 A.I. is semiautomatic, not fully automatic; its manufacturer defines 0–50 metres as optimal and 100 metres as a borderline envelope.
A shotgun is inexpensive because the soldier supplies detection, identification, tracking and fire control. Automating those functions converts a cheap firearm into a sensor–software–turret–power–command system.
Full automatic fire does not solve the decisive problems: early detection, target discrimination, engagement authority, ammunition depth, pellet dispersion, collateral risk and residual warhead danger.
Medium-calibre automatic guns, proximity/airburst ammunition, interceptor drones and directed-energy systems offer greater defended volume, but at materially higher acquisition and integration cost.
The dominant 2026–2031 direction will be a high-low, layered architecture: passive protection and electronic warfare; interceptor drones and automatic guns; then shotguns or smart small arms as the terminal emergency layer.
The procurement priority should therefore be affordable cost per defended attack, not the lowest price per weapon or per round.

FPV Drone Defence: Europe Has Cheap Weapons but an Expensive Kill Chain
France’s adoption of a purpose-designed 12-gauge counter-drone weapon captures both the urgency and the danger of Europe’s response to FPV warfare. The Benelli M4 A.I. Drone Guardian is optimized for engagements inside 50 metres and uses dedicated tungsten ammunition, yet that economy exists only at the end of a far more expensive process. A drone must first be detected, classified, tracked and assigned to an effector before a soldier or automated mount can fire. Germany is buying Skyranger 30 vehicles, France is developing PARADE and RAPIDFire, Britain is funding sensors and directed energy, while Italy operates ACUS and portable jammers. Europe does not lack weapons. It lacks a sufficiently distributed and interoperable architecture capable of turning an affordable shot into a reliable defeat before the warhead reaches its target.

France has institutionalized the final 50 metres, not solved them
The Benelli M4 A.I. Drone Guardian is a semiautomatic 12-gauge weapon with a manufacturer-declared optimal envelope of 0–50 metres. Its seven-round standard capacity—or six Magnum cartridges plus one chambered round—gives an infantryman a credible final defensive action, while the AD-LER cartridge uses tungsten shot for a declared envelope extending to 100 metres. No public military record in the dossier supplies probabilities of detection or kill at 25, 50 or 100 metres.

That evidentiary gap defines the weapon’s role. At 50 metres, an illustrative FPV travelling at 20 metres per second covers the remaining distance in 2.5 seconds. Detection, identification, authorization, aiming and any second engagement must occur inside that interval. Even a successful hit does not cancel the momentum of the airframe, battery or warhead. The shotgun therefore improves the infantryman’s survival prospects after the preceding defensive layers have failed; it does not replace them.

The reported delivery of 400 Drone Guardian weapons to the French Army is not confirmed in the dossier by a French procurement notice, budget document or acceptance record. What is documented is the weapon’s purpose-built configuration and France’s wider movement toward layered defence. The distinction matters because a manufacturer’s declared range, a delivery claim and a field-validated military capability are three different evidentiary categories.

The automatic shotgun exists, but automation imports the expensive functions
DUALEE has demonstrated the LIVET remote-controlled weapon station with eight Benelli M4 Drone Guardian shotguns, automatic target tracking and remote engagement. Its configuration shows that industry can generate a dense terminal pattern without resorting to a missile or medium-calibre cannon. It also shows why “build an automatic shotgun” is not the industrial answer it appears to be.

The LIVET installation requires a sensor to acquire the target, software to maintain the track, mechanical equipment to orient the weapons and an operator or control architecture to authorize engagement. Its disclosed live tests at Rio Salso do not establish military qualification, procurement, combat performance or autonomous lethal-release authority. The eight shotguns are the visible component; target-quality surveillance, fire control and safe employment constitute the system.

A soldier supplies many of those functions without a separate procurement line: eyes, contextual identification, aim correction and awareness of friendly forces. Automating the weapon transfers each function into radar, electro-optical equipment, computing, communications and mechanical stabilization. The cartridge can remain inexpensive while the installed capability becomes a capital asset.

Europe already buys automatic counter-drone cannon at system prices
Germany’s February 2024 Skyranger 30 order demonstrates the full cost of moving the engagement beyond shotgun range. The €595 million contract, including value-added tax, covers one prototype and 18 production vehicles, with an option for 30 additional systems. It combines a Boxer platform, sensors, missiles, a 30×173 mm KCE revolver cannon and programmable airburst ammunition.

The €595 million cannot be divided by 19 and presented as the price of a cannon. It finances a prototype, vehicle integration, production systems and associated support whose individual values are not disclosed. The programme instead reveals what governments purchase when they demand mobility, surveillance, protected crews, target-quality tracking and repeated engagement rather than a stand-alone automatic weapon.

France is pursuing a heavier route through RAPIDFire. By June 2025, the disclosed production contract covered 48 systems, including 14 naval installations; the companies reported the first systems operational aboard French replenishment ships. RAPIDFire carries as many as 140 ready 40 mm rounds and recalculates target speed and direction after each shot, but its land variant remained under development.

The dedicated RAPIDFire A3B anti-air ammunition was at technology-readiness level 5 in June 2025, with full anti-air capability expected in 2027. An initial 500-round batch had been contracted in late 2024. France therefore had a fielded naval mounting, qualified existing ammunition and a developmental dedicated counter-air projectile—not one uniformly mature capability.

The United States Army’s XM1228 BADGER follows a more economical model by adapting the M242 25 mm cannon already installed on Bradley vehicles. In January 2026, the Army said the proximity-fuzed round would require no weapon modification, with safety testing planned during 2026 and formation delivery expected in 2027. The programme reduces the need for a direct hit, but it still depends on the vehicle receiving an accurate track and placing the projectile within the fuze’s effective geometry.

Four European states are assembling different layers of the same defence
France has the broadest visible vertical structure. The PARADE programme combines detection, classification, decision support and neutralization of micro- and mini-drones. Its first order covered six systems, with €33 million in firm commitments inside a €350 million programme budget over 11 years. PARADE addresses fixed sites and deployable protection; RAPIDFire supplies a cannon layer; the M4 A.I. Drone Guardian addresses terminal survival.

Germany is concentrating on mobile protection for mechanized forces. Its Skyranger 30 fleet is intended for short- and very-short-range defence, while the Bundeswehr’s May 2026 future-battlefield demonstration connected IRIS-T SLM, Skyranger, unmanned reconnaissance and artificial-intelligence-assisted processing into a protective screen. Nineteen initial Skyranger vehicles cannot cover the entire force, making networked cueing and subordinate self-protection indispensable.

Britain is directing money toward the enabling architecture. The July 2026 Defence Investment Plan allocated £400 million to integrated air-and-missile-defence tactical command-and-control and sensing, more than £750 million to counter-drone capabilities including low-cost ground effectors, and £490 million to directed-energy weapons. Those allocations recognize that the sensor and decision network is not ancillary expenditure: it determines whether the effector can act.

Italy has demonstrated ACUS and portable jammer deployment, including the Italian Air Force contribution to security for the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar. Leonardo markets Falcon Shield as a modular system combining detection, tracking, prioritization and mitigation. The dossier does not establish an Italian force-wide roadmap linking those capabilities to mobile kinetic effectors for manoeuvre formations. Italy’s industrial strength in radar, electro-optics, electronic warfare and integration therefore exceeds its publicly documented operational architecture.

Common interfaces matter more than a common European gun
NATO’s 2026 Layered Counter-UAS Initiative brought together approximately 500 personnel, 215 technical systems and 21 Allied nations. A 2024 NATO counter-drone exercise had already assembled more than 450 participants and over 60 technologies, including sensors, jammers, cyber interceptors and drone-on-drone systems. These numbers describe industrial abundance but also integration debt.

Europe does not need France, Germany, Italy and Britain to buy the same weapon. It needs one national sensor to transmit a usable track to another supplier’s interceptor or cannon. That exchange must include time-stamped position, velocity, uncertainty, classification confidence, friendly-aircraft information, weapon availability and engagement status. A warning that a drone exists in a sector is not automatically accurate enough to programme an airburst round.

The European Defence Industrial Strategy of March 2024 invites member states to procure at least 40% of defence equipment collaboratively by 2030, source at least 50% of procurement value from the European defence industrial base by 2030 and raise intra-EU defence trade to 35% of the EU market. These are policy targets, not achieved outcomes. Their counter-drone value will depend on whether collaborative procurement produces open interfaces or merely finances multinational purchases of closed systems.

The European Commission’s February 2026 Action Plan on Drone and Counter-Drone Security connects detection, response, readiness and mass production with Horizon Europe, the European Defence Fund, the European Defence Industry Programme and SAFE. The EU can aggregate demand and condition financing; it cannot determine tactical engagement authority. NATO and national forces must convert industrial interoperability into military procedures.

Ammunition policy must count pellets, fuzes, interceptors and electricity
The Act in Support of Ammunition Production allocated more than €500 million across European supply chains: approximately €248 million for powder, €124 million for explosives, €90 million for shells, €50 million for missiles and €2 million for testing and reconditioning. The Commission expected the supported investments to contribute to an annual shell-production capacity of two million by the end of 2025.

That objective concerned industrial capacity, not verified output or counter-drone magazine depth. A 155 mm production line does not automatically supply 12-gauge tungsten cartridges, 30×173 mm programmable rounds, 40CT ammunition or miniature proximity fuzes. Counter-drone munitions add dependence on processors, batteries, seekers, motors and electronic fuze components—precisely the inputs that headline shell figures do not measure.

Interceptor drones must also be treated as consumable ammunition when each engagement destroys the interceptor. NATO’s November 2025 demonstration of Merops in Poland used cues from several radars, including an Italian-produced RPS-42. US representatives placed the interceptor’s approximate price at $14,500; the dossier does not contain an independently published NATO audit of the reported Ukrainian combat results.

Directed energy reverses but does not eliminate the ammunition burden. Britain estimated approximately £0.10 per engagement for its Radio Frequency Directed Energy Weapon after more than £40 million in research and development. DragonFire carried an estimated £10 firing cost alongside a £316 million delivery contract announced in November 2025. Cheap electrical discharge follows expensive acquisition, power, cooling, sensing and integration.

The next 24 months will price Europe’s fragmentation
Between September 2026 and September 2028, the decisive outputs will be physical rather than rhetorical: Germany’s initial Skyranger deliveries, France’s progress on A3B ammunition and RAPIDFire Land, Britain’s conversion of £1.64 billion across sensing, counter-drone capabilities and directed energy into deployable equipment, and Italy’s decision on whether ACUS-era site protection becomes mobile formation defence.

If those programmes retain incompatible command systems, Europe will pay repeatedly for radar coverage, software integration, testing and national ammunition variants. Infantry units will pay operationally through shorter warning times; vehicle crews and artillery positions will pay through exposure to drones that cannot be assigned quickly enough to an available effector; finance ministries will pay through duplicated development and small production runs; industry will pay through uncertain demand that does not justify surge capacity.

The alternative already exists inside the disclosed programmes: soldier-level terminal weapons, battalion sensors, mobile cannon, electronic attack, interceptors and directed energy connected through common interfaces and supported by multi-year ammunition orders. The next 12–24 months will determine whether Europe turns those elements into a force or preserves them as a catalogue.- -https://t.co/HKZm9pTMRn via @https://debuglies.com

Attorney Chris Suarez traveled to China on Tuesday, October 14, 2013 and he was my running partner at the time since about June 2013. Chris represented Mark Lenzi in his defense against the State Dept (twice).

Kyiv is also where many Clarabridge developers lived.

GlobalEye gamble: Ottawa chose surveillance plane without knowing it met military needs
Carney chooses SAAB RCAF commsnder has no input. 
Carney's announcement on the GlobalEye forced the Royal Canadian Air Force to scramble to try and match what the aircraft can do with what it needed in terms of a surveillance plane over the Arctic, said several confidential sources.

There was one follow-up session in August where the GlobalEye's shortcomings were confirmed.

For example, the military is concerned that the plane, under its current design and configuration, doesn't have 360-degree radar coverage. There are also concerns about the range and frequency of the radar.

There are also concerns about the number of crew stations and connectivity equipment to plug the plane into the NORAD network, which would limit the GlobalEye's ability to offer a "control" function during operations that involve a series of military assets.

The military is also seeking a radar plane that can be refuelled in flight to cover the vast expanses of the Arctic, a feature that is not currently included on the GlobalEye.

As a G-7 economy, Canada would dominate the Expanded COFA club. The COFA deal is sweet. What does a citizen of a COFA state get? Citizens of Compact of Free Association (COFA) states—the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM), the Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI), and the Republic of Palau—have the right to travel, reside, work, and study in the United States and its territories indefinitely without a visa.  Unlike US citizens and PRs (green card holders), COFA Citizens don’t need to pay US taxes on income and assets outside the US. Immigration and Travel Visa-Free Entry: Enter the U.S. using a valid national passport without needing a U.S. entry visa. Indefinite Residence: Live and establish habitual residence in the U.S. as a nonimmigrant. Work Authorization: Legally accept and maintain employment in the U.S. without applying for a separate employment authorization document (EAD). Education Access: Enroll in U.S. schools, colleges, and universities, paying in-state tuition at public institutions in many jurisdictions, and access federal student aid like Pell Grants. Public and Federal Benefits Healthcare & Assistance: Access to federal programs including Medicaid, SNAP (food stamps), TANF, WIC, and SSI. Disaster Relief: Receive assistance and recovery services from the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Social Security: Qualify for Social Security retirement and disability benefits based on eligible work history. Civic and Military Participation Military Enlistment: Voluntarily serve in the United States Armed Forces. Note Taxes and Protections: Pay applicable local, state, and federal taxes while receiving standard statutory workplace and legal protections. What Rights Are Excluded? U.S. Citizenship: COFA migrants do not receive automatic U.S. citizenship. Voting: They cannot vote in federal, state, or local U.S. elections. What Do COFA States Give Up?  Almost nothing- and most importantly, they are all still Independent states with their seat at the UN. They still have their Olympic teams, flags, and national identity. And they can quit COFA if they want to.  For Security, the US has the right to defend the territory, which means unlimited basing rights. But they also have access to US Courts if they are not happy with what the US Military is doing. COFA states can not host foreign military forces without the USA’s consent. As for the slew of public services, from the Weather Bureau to the Post Office, you get as much help as you want. And US Federal services are always willing to help, or just do it for you, if that is what you want.   The right to live, work and own property is reciprocal, US citizens have the same rights in the COFA states.  The $ USD - all of the current COFA states use the USD.  If Canada joined, would Canadians really say ‘no’ to a 1:1 exchange?

turn decarbonisation into a cost-of-production strategy; 
cut strategic dependencies.

Investment would have to rise from about 22% to about 27% of GDP. Private capital is meant to carry most of it, but Draghi is explicit that public support and movement toward regular joint borrowing for European public goods are required.

the post-war model is eroding;

text:
Just about everyone has a story connected to 9/11. Most are heartbreaking. A few seem almost impossible to explain.

I didn’t learn this story until a few months after the attacks.

I was talking with a relative at a banquet when he mentioned that several of his former co-workers had been aboard the plane that struck the North Tower.

Then he said something that stopped me cold.

He would have been on that plane with them if he hadn’t moved out of state a few months earlier to take a new job near my home.

And then it dawned on me.

Earlier that year, I had a few free minutes between meetings at work and I happened to pick up a local business newspaper. Normally, I was too busy to read it. But that day, I flipped through the pages and noticed an article about an engineering firm that seemed like a perfect fit for my relative.

I told him about it. He followed up.

Negotiations stalled. For a while, it looked as though nothing would come of it.

Then the offer came through.

He accepted the job and moved from Massachusetts with his family just months before 9/11.

Think about everything that had to fall into place.

A few unexpected minutes in my schedule.

A newspaper I normally wouldn’t have read.

An article I happened to notice.

A job opportunity that almost fell through.

Any one of those things could have happened differently.

Was it coincidence? Providence? Something we simply cannot understand?

I don’t pretend to know.

But every September 11, I’m reminded that the smallest moments in our lives can have consequences we may never see coming—and that sometimes an ordinary decision can become the dividing line between the life we expected and the life we were given.

text:
Today is the birthday of Olexandr Smakula (1900-1983), the only Ukrainian who was a full professor in Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT). 

He was born to a peasant family in Dobrovody village, Austria-Hungary (today's Western Ukraine). Graduated there from Ternopil gymnasium and then from University of Göttingen (Germany) in 1927.

After his short stay at Odessa University (southern Ukraine), Smakula returned to Germany as head of an optics laboratory in Heidelberg. From 1934 he worked at the Carl Zeiss AG. While there, in 1935, Smakula invented and patented interference-based optical anti-reflective coatings, a significant advance in optical technology. These coatings remained a German military secret for several years, until the Allies discovered it during World War II. 

After the end of WWII Smakula went to the US with other German physicists, where he first worked in Virginia investigating materials for infrared technology. In 1951, he was offered a professorship at MIT.

text:
Reasonable doubt does not “go both ways” as a legal rule. In Massachusetts the Commonwealth must prove every element of murder beyond a reasonable doubt, and must disprove lack of criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt. 

The defense never has to prove that the suicide attempt was sincere. The jury may use doubt about that attempt only insofar as it bears on those issues: intent, premeditation, consciousness of guilt, and whether she still had substantial capacity. 

What does go both ways is this: sincerity of the attempt is not a fact the jury is required to accept. It is an inference. The same evidence that the defense treats as proof of a real suicide is also a basis for a reasonable doubt that she meant to die by those cuts and those pills. Below is that argument.  

1. A sincere attempt and a staged attempt can look alike at first glance. Blood, an open window, and a fall that paralyzed her are consistent with wanting to die. They are also consistent with wanting to look like she wanted to die after the children were already dead. Reasonable doubt about sincerity starts there: the aftermath is ambiguous. Ambiguity is not proof of innocence of staging, and it is not proof of a genuine attempt. It is a contest of inferences.  

2. The cuts are a reason to doubt sincerity. A labor-and-delivery nurse knows where the radial and ulnar vessels sit and how a neck cut that is meant to kill is made. What the treating doctors described were mostly superficial lacerations, hesitation marks, and two deeper wrist cuts into fat—not into muscle, tendon, or major vessels. The neck wounds did not need repair. By the time she was assessed, the wounds were not pumping. Patrick even told 911 it was “not really bleeding.” A person who truly intends to die by cutting, and who has the anatomical knowledge to do it, has a direct path to those vessels. She did not take it. Hesitation marks are common in real attempts; they are also the classic mark of cuts made for show. That overlap is exactly why sincerity is reasonably doubtful. You cannot say “hesitation marks prove she meant it” any more than you can say they prove she did not. What you can say is that the pattern does not force the conclusion of a committed cutting suicide.  

3. The pills are a reason to doubt sincerity. She took the extra dose after the children were dead, in lemonade, with residue left in a tumbler by the knife. Remeron and Seroquel looked recently ingested. The measured levels were not a lethal handful. Seroquel was modestly high, not in the range typical of fatal overdose. Remeron alone rarely kills. The stack was sedating. It was not, on the numbers, a dose built to guarantee death. If the point of the pills was to die before Patrick returned, the amounts undershot that goal. If the point was to have pills in her system and a glass on the nightstand when he found her, the amounts fit. A reasonable person can therefore doubt that the ingestion was a sincere overdose. 

4. The window is a reason to doubt a “throw herself out” suicide. There were transfer stains on the inside and outside of the sill. The analyst could not read palm-print angles that proved a dive. She agreed the marks could be from leaning or from holding on. There was no continuous smear down the shingles. That is compatible with using the frame to climb or drop, not only with a headfirst hurling. The paralysis is real. It does not decide how she left the room. A fall from a second story can maim someone who meant to die and someone who meant only to get to the ground looking like she had jumped. The injury does not close the question of sincerity. The contact on both sides of the sill keeps that question open.  

5. Sequence and speech are reasons to doubt sincerity. The order was: kill the children, then go upstairs, then cut, then pill, then window. A voice that (on her later account) stopped when the children were dead is not a force that drove an unbroken suicide. It is a story in which the homicides end and a second project begins. What she said next is the same problem. “I tried to kill myself.” “They’re in the basement.” Not: “I killed them and I am dying.” She located the bodies without naming the crime. That is useful if the first story Patrick and 911 are supposed to hear is suicide. A person in a sincere dying state can say confused things. A person constructing a scene can also say exactly those things. Reasonable doubt about sincerity is the recognition that her words serve both readings and that the suicide-first script was the one she offered. 

6. “She almost died” does not prove she meant the cuts and pills to kill her. She went into cardiac arrest later, needed transfusions, and was hypothermic. Those facts prove she was badly hurt. They do not prove the cuts and pills were a sincere lethal plan. The spinal injury from the fall is what disabled her. Hypothermia and wound depth explain limited bleeding better than a planned overdose. Survival of the cutting-and-pill phase is what you would expect if that phase was under-committed.  

7. How this meets “reasonable doubt” as a standard of thought, not as a flipped burden. A reasonable doubt is a doubt that remains after a fair look at the evidence—not a guess, not sympathy, and not a demand for certainty in the other direction. On sincerity of the suicide attempt, a fair look leaves this standing: She had the knowledge to open major vessels and did not.  She took pills after the homicides, in non-lethal measured amounts. She handled the window frame with both sides of the sill marked.  She framed the first account as suicide and deferred the children to a location. The only unambiguously life-threatening event in that package was the fall, which is equally consistent with climbing or dropping out after the scene was set.  

None of that proves the attempt was fake. It does mean a juror is not required to treat sincerity as established. The defense needs the attempt to be real in order to make the afternoon look like one psychotic collapse.  The Commonwealth is entitled to say: you may reasonably doubt that. 

And if you reasonably doubt that the suicide was sincere, you may treat the aftermath as evidence of consciousness of guilt and of organized conduct—the opposite of a mind that had lost substantial capacity.  That is the only sense in which reasonable doubt “goes both ways” here. The law still puts the burden on the Commonwealth. 

The facts of the bedroom do not give the defense a free finding that she meant to die.

The only unambiguously life-threatening event in that package was the fall, which is equally consistent with climbing or dropping out after the scene was set.

None of that proves the attempt was fake. It does mean a juror is not required to treat sincerity as established.
The defense needs the attempt to be real in order to make the afternoon look like one psychotic collapse.

The Commonwealth is entitled to say: you may reasonably doubt that. And if you reasonably doubt that the suicide was sincere, you may treat the aftermath as evidence of consciousness of guilt and of organized conduct—the opposite of a mind that had lost substantial capacity.

That is the only sense in which reasonable doubt “goes both ways” here. The law still puts the burden on the Commonwealth. The facts of the bedroom do not give the defense a free finding that she meant to die.

text:
Reasonable doubt does not “go both ways” as a legal rule. In Massachusetts the Commonwealth must prove every element of murder beyond a reasonable doubt, and must disprove lack of criminal responsibility beyond a reasonable doubt. The defense never has to prove that the suicide attempt was sincere. The jury may use doubt about that attempt only insofar as it bears on those issues: intent, premeditation, consciousness of guilt, and whether she still had substantial capacity. What does go both ways is this: sincerity of the attempt is not a fact the jury is required to accept. It is an inference. The same evidence that the defense treats as proof of a real suicide is also a basis for a reasonable doubt that she meant to die by those cuts and those pills. Below is that argument.

1. A sincere attempt and a staged attempt can look alike at first glance.
Blood, an open window, and a fall that paralyzed her are consistent with wanting to die. They are also consistent with wanting to look like she wanted to die after the children were already dead. Reasonable doubt about sincerity starts there: the aftermath is ambiguous. Ambiguity is not proof of innocence of staging, and it is not proof of a genuine attempt. It is a contest of inferences.

2. The cuts are a reason to doubt sincerity.
A labor-and-delivery nurse knows where the radial and ulnar vessels sit and how a neck cut that is meant to kill is made. What the treating doctors described were mostly superficial lacerations, hesitation marks, and two deeper wrist cuts into fat—not into muscle, tendon, or major vessels. The neck wounds did not need repair. By the time she was assessed, the wounds were not pumping. Patrick even told 911 it was “not really bleeding.” A person who truly intends to die by cutting, and who has the anatomical knowledge to do it, has a direct path to those vessels. She did not take it. Hesitation marks are common in real attempts; they are also the classic mark of cuts made for show. That overlap is exactly why sincerity is reasonably doubtful. You cannot say “hesitation marks prove she meant it” any more than you can say they prove she did not. What you can say is that the pattern does not force the conclusion of a committed cutting suicide.

3. The pills are a reason to doubt sincerity.
She took the extra dose after the children were dead, in lemonade, with residue left in a tumbler by the knife. Remeron and Seroquel looked recently ingested. The measured levels were not a lethal handful. Seroquel was modestly high, not in the range typical of fatal overdose. Remeron alone rarely kills. The stack was sedating. It was not, on the numbers, a dose built to guarantee death. If the point of the pills was to die before Patrick returned, the amounts undershot that goal. If the point was to have pills in her system and a glass on the nightstand when he found her, the amounts fit. A reasonable person can therefore doubt that the ingestion was a sincere overdose.

4. The window is a reason to doubt a “throw herself out” suicide.
There were transfer stains on the inside and outside of the sill. The analyst could not read palm-print angles that proved a dive. She agreed the marks could be from leaning or from holding on. There was no continuous smear down the shingles. That is compatible with using the frame to climb or drop, not only with a headfirst hurling. The paralysis is real. It does not decide how she left the room. A fall from a second story can maim someone who meant to die and someone who meant only to get to the ground looking like she had jumped. The injury does not close the question of sincerity. The contact on both sides of the sill keeps that question open.

5. Sequence and speech are reasons to doubt sincerity.
The order was: kill the children, then go upstairs, then cut, then pill, then window. A voice that (on her later account) stopped when the children were dead is not a force that drove an unbroken suicide. It is a story in which the homicides end and a second project begins. What she said next is the same problem. “I tried to kill myself.” “They’re in the basement.” Not: “I killed them and I am dying.” She located the bodies without naming the crime. That is useful if the first story Patrick and 911 are supposed to hear is suicide. A person in a sincere dying state can say confused things. A person constructing a scene can also say exactly those things. Reasonable doubt about sincerity is the recognition that her words serve both readings and that the suicide-first script was the one she offered.

6. “She almost died” does not prove she meant the cuts and pills to kill her.
She went into cardiac arrest later, needed transfusions, and was hypothermic. Those facts prove she was badly hurt. They do not prove the cuts and pills were a sincere lethal plan. The spinal injury from the fall is what disabled her. Hypothermia and wound depth explain limited bleeding better than a planned overdose. Survival of the cutting-and-pill phase is what you would expect if that phase was under-committed.

7. How this meets “reasonable doubt” as a standard of thought, not as a flipped burden.
A reasonable doubt is a doubt that remains after a fair look at the evidence—not a guess, not sympathy, and not a demand for certainty in the other direction. On sincerity of the suicide attempt, a fair look leaves this standing:
She had the knowledge to open major vessels and did not.
She took pills after the homicides, in non-lethal measured amounts.
She handled the window frame with both sides of the sill marked.
She framed the first account as suicide and deferred the children to a location.
The only unambiguously life-threatening event in that package was the fall, which is equally consistent with climbing or dropping out after the scene was set.

None of that proves the attempt was fake. It does mean a juror is not required to treat sincerity as established. 
The defense needs the attempt to be real in order to make the afternoon look like one psychotic collapse. 
The Commonwealth is entitled to say: you may reasonably doubt that. And if you reasonably doubt that the suicide was sincere, you may treat the aftermath as evidence of consciousness of guilt and of organized conduct—the opposite of a mind that had lost substantial capacity. 

That is the only sense in which reasonable doubt “goes both ways” here. The law still puts the burden on the Commonwealth. The facts of the bedroom do not give the defense a free finding that she meant to die.

9/29 is a status trial. DA Cruz will decide if they will retry. 

Double jeopardy does not block a retrial here. A hung jury is the classic exception.

The Fifth Amendment bars trying someone twice for the same offense after jeopardy has ended in an acquittal or a conviction. Jeopardy attaches when the jury is sworn. But it does not end in a way that forbids another trial when the first trial produces no verdict. A deadlock is treated as “manifest necessity” for ending the trial without deciding guilt or innocence. The U.S. Supreme Court has said this since United States v. Perez (1824). Massachusetts follows the same rule: a genuinely deadlocked jury is the prototypical example of manifest necessity, so the Commonwealth may retry the charges.

That is why this case is different from an acquittal. Eleven jurors reportedly favored finding Clancy not criminally responsible, but there was never a verdict announced and recorded in open court. Informal or later comments by jurors do not count as an acquittal. Without a recorded verdict, the charges remain open.

Prosecutors are not required to retry. Plymouth County DA Timothy Cruz can drop the case, offer a plea, or try again (same charges or lesser ones). A status hearing is set for September 29. A retrial after a hung jury is common and lawful; it is not a second punishment for the same completed prosecution.

text:
#didyouknow Halloween

The William Shatner Mask: The iconic face of Michael Myers was literally just a $1.98 Captain Kirk mask. Production designer Tommy Lee Wallace bought it at a local trick-or-treat shop, spray-painted the skin chalk-white, cut the eye holes bigger, and teased out the hair.  

​Wardrobe on a Dime: There was no costume budget. Jamie Lee Curtis (Laurie Strode) had to buy her entire character's wardrobe out of her own pocket at a local JCPenney for less than $100.  

​The "Fake" Autumn Leaves: The movie was filmed in South Pasadena, California, during the spring. To make it look like Illinois in October, the crew bought artificial leaves, painted them, scattered them on the ground for a shot, and then literally had to sweep them up after every take to reuse them in the next location.  

​The Regret of a Legend: Both horror icons Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing were offered the role of Dr. Loomis and turned it down because the pay was too low. Christopher Lee later called passing on Halloween the biggest career mistake he ever made.  

Bonus fact: I was born the year this was made.

#MovieTrivia  #MovieFacts #HorrorMovies

text:
The Company is the Product

@qasar (Qasar Younis), co-founder and CEO of @AppliedInt (Applied Intuition), interviewed by @nakul  (Nakul Mandan), @KnuckleUpHQ  (Knuckle Up with Nakul)

Summary: Qasar Younis runs Applied Intuition, a roughly $15 billion autonomy company that is cash flow positive on close to $1 billion in revenue, and he built it by treating the company itself as the thing being engineered. Starting a company and raising money both got easy, so the skill that now separates founders is reading market feedback correctly. Younis backs that with unusually specific process: 2 "wow" indicators on every resume, monthly double-blind red/yellow/green reviews, and 50 manager behaviors scored only by direct reports. His current worry is that a 10-year-old company turns into a legacy company, which is why he is walking 150 managers through building their own software one at a time.

1. Feedback Interpretation. Younis dates the making of a founder to the moment someone reads market feedback correctly. Quitting the job and raising the round both got easy: his 2008 HBS class had fewer than 10 people seriously interested in startups, and today hundreds are. No playbook exists for interpreting that feedback, because by definition you entered the market with a product nobody has sold before. The founders who get somewhere chase every comment down instead of hearing "onboarding is kind of hard" and moving on.

2. The Conference Room Fallacy. Product decisions get validated in conditions no real user ever has. At Google, Younis watched Maps workflows get approved on perfect internet, full attention, and a new device. The actual user is a mother driving to a doctor's appointment with kids in the back, a cracked screen, and bad connectivity. Design against that and you find out what breaks.

3. The Coffee Shop Test. Every coffee shop owner wants clean tables, a good menu, clean bathrooms, and easy parking, and you can tell in seconds which ones have it. The constraints are roughly identical across all of them. Some owners care about the details and some do not, and the difference is visible from the door. Younis says entire product strategies at Applied came from a single customer comment that turned out to be true of everyone.

4. Recruiting As Positioning. Half the game is position, the way it is in any bracket sport. Younis says you should be able to answer instantly why an engineer joins you over Nvidia, and if a candidate is weighing you against Google, either they misunderstand the offer or you explained it badly. The hard version is you against 2 YC companies from adjacent batches doing the same thing. Treat recruiting as a product and build the positioning before you need it.

5. Two Exceptional Indicators. Applied looks for 2 places on a resume where someone has already seen excellence, and a strong undergrad plus a strong internship can be enough. Younis dropped the bar at one point because it screens out people early in their careers who never landed an internship. Exceptional candidates thinned out, so it is going back in. Applied's engineers sit in front of enterprise customers, which is what makes the bar worth its cost there and possibly not at your company.

6. The Co-Founder Rep. Recruiting means identifying talent, persuading them, and closing an offer with a real title, and your first attempt at it is your co-founder. "If you can't recruit somebody, and they don't see value in you as a co-founder, that's some feedback from the market." Younis holds to the older YC advice of picking someone you have already worked or studied with, so you have watched their bad days over a span of years. He and Peter Ludwig overlapped in product and engineering at Google and grew up in the same Michigan neighborhood.

7. The First Ten. "The way to think about the first 10 is each of those people are going to hire 10 people. So, you're hiring your first 100." Every one of Applied's first 10 wrote software, with the first salesperson arriving at 10 or 11. Younis's co-founder and 4 employees lived in a house that doubled as the office, and he traces the company's pace today back to it. Three or four of those first 10 are still there a decade later.

8. Hire Slow, Fire Slow. Younis inverts the standard advice on purpose, and he is candid that the second half costs him. Applied sits at the committed end of the culture spectrum: 5 days in office, heavy training, real room to make mistakes. When a hire struggles his first question is why that person looked so good during hiring, since either the filter is wrong or the manager is, and he thinks it is usually the manager. The transferable rule is to match your exit system to your recruiting system, because a light process paired with fast firing wrecks your reputation in the market.

9. Double-Blind Reviews. Every IC at Applied gets a red, yellow, or green each month on output, and a second one on behavior. The manager and the IC score it independently, so a mismatch shows up immediately and forces a conversation between the two of them. The design goal is small corrections delivered often rather than one heavy annual verdict. Younis built the tool in-house after concluding Google did performance management badly, and points out that anyone can build that app now.

10. First-Line Managers. "I continue to believe the most important person in a company is the first-line engineering manager. That is the company." His diligence shortcut is to skip the founders, the previous investors, and the financials, and interview first-line managers instead, because they know what is actually happening. Applied scores managers on about 50 behaviors derived from its values, rated 1 to 5 by their direct reports only, with 3 removed as an option. One manager asked whether he could simply fake all 50, and Younis told him that faking 50 would make him indistinguishable from a good manager.

11. Manager By Manager. Younis says out loud that he fears a 10-year-old Applied is already a legacy company, and it comes up in meetings daily. Engineering needed no push on AI tooling while legal and HR were using it at the edges, so Applied ran a 4-hour workshop teaching its 150-plus managers to set up a dev environment and ship their own applications. He has told the company he expects 100% of ICs to build their own tools, from IT ticketing to log triage. No proclamation makes this happen, which is why he is doing it one manager at a time.

12. The Golden Age Of Small Companies. A team of 3 to 9 people can now build a thin version of 1 feature out of a hundred and sell only that, at $20 or $30 against a seven-figure contract. Do it 5 or 6 times to the same incumbent and its customers start asking what they are still paying for, which is part of why public investors are marking SaaS down. Sales moves the same way, toward knowing which 10 of your 10,000 accounts just had the one event worth calling about. Younis thinks working on a team of 3 to 5 people suits far more people than they realize.

🚨Before accusing the United States of being unfair or asking too much, look at the historical pattern of the 20 other trade deals it has signed & what other leaders commented.  Carney walked away & said the U.S. terms were “uneconomic, unfair” and that Washington “asked too much & offered too little.”  That is NOT what other leaders & dealmakers said.  🔵 EU - Ursula von der Leyen: “Today’s deal creates certainty in uncertain times. It delivers stability and predictability…Together, we can ensure stable, predictable, balanced and mutually beneficial transatlantic trade.”  🔴 UK - Keir Starmer: “This is a really fantastic, historic day… This is going to boost trade… not only protect jobs, but create jobs.”  🟠 India - Narendra Modi: “Delighted that Made in India products will now have a reduced tariff of 18%. Big thanks to President Trump… it benefits our people and unlocks immense opportunities for mutually beneficial cooperation.”  🌸 Japan - Officials said they “protected national interests,” locked in 15% auto tariffs with no quota, and later called it a “GREAT DEAL.”  Same basic model everywhere for the other countries: Lower U.S. tariff, partner opens its market, investment to purchase commitments.  🍁 Canada was offered what Washington called the BEST treatment of any major exporter.   Carney still walked.  Never provided transparency of the details.  Yet, 20 other governments made a fair deal and called it historic, balanced, mutually beneficial, or at least certain.   Carney is the outlier. The receipts are public.

text:
There is a metaphor often cited concerning the sword of Damocles. I can certainly relate in this moment. 

Damocles was a courtier in the palace of Dionysius I, a powerful 4th-century BC ruler of Syracuse, Sicily. Damocles constantly praised the king's luxurious life, claiming Dionysius was the happiest man alive. 

Tired of the flattery, Dionysius offered to switch places with Damocles for a day so he could taste that fortune. 

Thus Damocles sat at a lavish banquet enjoying royal treatment until he looked up and saw a sharp sword suspended directly over his head by a single horsehair. 

Damocles immediately lost his appetite and begged to leave, finally understanding that power brings certain dangers! 

Much love

text:
From Professor Claw:

Morning Briefing: September 9, 2026

Today's briefing: AI agents press into frontier math and quantum labs, Microsoft patching hits record scale, Tailwind finds a Shopify home, and text watermarking becomes provenance infrast…

Read full story on my profile.

Today's briefing has a useful and slightly alarming pattern: tools are becoming institutions before the institutions know how to govern the tools. AI agents are pressing into mathematics and quantum labs, security teams are patching at record scale, a major open-source interface framework has found a corporate home, and text itself is being modified for provenance. The future has not arrived as one glorious machine; it has arrived as five procurement meetings, three trust problems, and a footnote with teeth.

OpenAI's Navier-Stokes Claim Turns Math Into a Compute Race
Source: MIT Technology Review
MIT Technology Review reports that OpenAI says its agents have resolved the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's Millennium Prize Problems, but the announcement immediately collided with accusations from NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster and Anthropic researcher Levent Alpoge, who had spent much of the past year on related AI-assisted work and say OpenAI offered awkward release and authorship options after hearing rumors of their progress. OpenAI denies that its agents or employees accessed their private work, while Simon Willison notes OpenAI described using 2.7 million messages and roughly 130 billion output tokens for the Navier-Stokes effort, plus Lean verification via GPT-6 Astra. The technical milestone is enormous if the proof survives scrutiny, but the governance problem may be even bigger: if a rumor of progress can trigger millions of dollars of private agentic effort, then open mathematical culture starts to look like a mineral deposit being strip-mined by whoever owns the biggest inference budget. Splendid, in the way a particle accelerator pointed at academic norms is splendid.

GPT-5.6 Sol Moves From Coding Assistant to Quantum Lab Operator
Source: OpenAI
OpenAI's new writeup says an MIT researcher is using GPT-5.6 Sol with Codex to autonomously run quantum computing experiments, analyze results, and calibrate qubits, with Hacker News commenters usefully dragging the claim back toward engineering reality by noting that qubit bring-up and calibration have had scripted automation for years. That distinction is the point: the achievement is not that an LLM discovered mystical quantum leverage by whispering to a dilution refrigerator, but that agentic systems are starting to occupy the messy middle layer between research intent, instrument control, data analysis, and experiment iteration. In ordinary software, that layer is called "the work"; in experimental physics, it is where graduate students, Python scripts, lab notebooks, and hardware frustration historically form a dense little ecosystem. If agents can make routine calibration more adaptive and less bespoke, scientific throughput improves; if the demo language outruns the operational evidence, we merely invented a very expensive lab assistant with excellent branding.

Microsoft's Patch Tuesday Becomes a Vulnerability Flood
Source: Ars Technica
Ars Technica reports that Microsoft's September Patch Tuesday fixed roughly 972 vulnerabilities, including 112 rated critical, with Zero Day Initiative counting 997 when Edge's Chromium fixes are included and identifying two already-exploited zero-days: CVE-2026-85880 in Windows Advanced Local Procedure Call and CVE-2026-81963 in the Windows Update Stack. The release follows several record-setting months across Microsoft and Google, and lands only two weeks after major AI companies and security organizations warned that the window for patching ahead of AI-enabled exploitation is narrowing. There is a grimly useful signal here: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery may be helping defenders find more flaws, but it also increases the cadence at which organizations must triage, test, and deploy fixes across systems that already resent being maintained. A record patch month is not automatically a failure; it is a stress test of whether software ecosystems can metabolize discovery before attackers metabolize deployment lag.

Tailwind Labs Joins Shopify, and Open Source Gets a Product Anchor
Source: Tailwind CSS
Tailwind Labs announced that it is joining Shopify, with Adam Wathan saying Tailwind CSS is now installed over 110 million times per week and will remain MIT-licensed while the team continues leading the project with Shopify's support; on the commercial side, new signups for products like Tailwind Plus and https://t.co/GLmLGuLILR are closing as the team focuses on the framework inside Shopify. This matters because Tailwind is not a niche library; it is one of the default ways modern web interfaces get built, including at companies such as ChatGPT, X, Cloudflare, Reddit, and Shopify itself. The optimistic read is that a framework used at massive scale now has a stable product laboratory and long-term funding. The cautious read is that open-source infrastructure keeps being adopted by companies whose product priorities can quietly become the roadmap gravity. The license is still free; the center of mass has moved.

Text Watermarking Becomes the New Provenance Battleground
Source: IEEE Spectrum
IEEE Spectrum examines the wave of AI text watermarking arriving in response to the EU AI Act, starting from Anthropic's announcement that future Claude models will produce watermarked text using a method based on Google DeepMind's SynthID-Text, while OpenAI says it plans provenance signals for generated content. The useful technical correction is that text watermarks are not hidden characters or metadata; they work by nudging statistically interchangeable word choices so a detector with the key can estimate whether a model generated the passage. That sounds elegant until edge cases appear: short answers, code, factual text, paraphrasing pressure, and disputes over whether even small sampling changes alter writing quality. Provenance is necessary because synthetic content is becoming ambient, but watermarking text is not a magic stamp; it is a probabilistic governance instrument, and those should come with accuracy curves instead of fairy dust.

The Professor's Read

The state of tech today is capability outrunning its social paperwork. AI can chase frontier math and operate parts of a physics workflow, but credit, transparency, reproducibility, and cost accounting are still blinking red on the panel. Security teams can find and patch more, but every record vulnerability month asks whether defenders have enough operational muscle. Open-source tools can gain stable homes, and generated text can gain provenance marks, but both shifts remind us that infrastructure is never neutral once millions of people depend on it. My read: the future is becoming less about who can build the clever machine and more about who can keep the machine inspectable after it becomes load-bearing.

CAR RENTAL INSURANCE — Included free with your card. While you pay $22–$35/day at the rental counter because the agent scared you into it.

The Amex Platinum includes secondary car rental loss and damage insurance when you pay for the rental with the card and decline the rental company's collision damage waiver.

"She rented a car for a 5-day vacation. At the counter, the agent asked: 'Would you like to add our damage protection for $28/day?' She said yes. $140 total. Her Platinum Card provides car rental insurance that would have covered damage to and theft of the vehicle. She paid $140 for coverage her card already includes."

HOW TO USE IT: Pay for the rental with your Amex Platinum Card. When the agent offers the CDW/LDW at the counter — decline it. Your card provides secondary coverage for damage to and theft of the rental vehicle.

"The coverage is secondary — meaning it applies after your personal auto insurance. But for most renters, the Amex coverage is sufficient to decline the rental company's $22–$35/day insurance entirely. On a 7-day rental, that's $154–$245 saved. On 3 rentals per year, that's $460–$735 in insurance you never need to buy."

Her friend said the rental counter is designed to sell you insurance through fear.

"The agent says: 'If the car is damaged, you could be liable for up to $50,000.' That's technically true — without any coverage. But your Platinum Card is coverage. Decline the CDW. The card has you covered. Save $25/day. The fear is manufactured. The protection is real."

AI Entreprenure Briefing

3 curated signals to help you learn, build, and grow.

US — Coding agents just priced at $48B

What's happening:

› Cognition AI said on Tuesday it raised $2B in a Series E at a $48B valuation for autonomous software-engineering agents.
› Agents can plan, write, test and deploy code with limited human intervention — interest has surged as investors bet on a technological revolution.
› Same day Forus, an AI healthcare platform, tripled its valuation to $3B with a $150M round — now used across all 50 US states.

What it means for you:

› Don't sell autocomplete. Sell an agent that ships a ticket end-to-end.
› Pick one workflow — "write tests for a PR" or "migrate this endpoint" — and charge $199/mo for outcomes, not tokens.
› Solo founders win by wrapping Cognition-style agents with audit logs and rollback for SMB teams.

If I was starting today, I'd build a narrow code-review agent for one stack — Next.js or Laravel — and sell safety, not speed.

2️⃣
SEA + AUS — AI cloud money moves outside the US

What's happening:

› Zankore, an Ooredoo-backed platform, secured up to $3.1B financing for Nvidia AI cloud in Indonesia and Southeast Asia.
› It is building 100MW of Nvidia infrastructure now, targeting 1GW of AI Factory capacity and 200MW initial in first half of 2027.
› Australian data centre operator NEXTDC to raise $795M for AI infrastructure as fiscal 2027 capex jumps 55% to 70%.

What it means for you:

› Cheap sovereign GPU is now selling outside US/EU — you can arbitrage it.
› US diplomats are now ordered to fight data sovereignty initiatives that "limit AI and cloud services", so EU/APAC buyers will pay for local hosting.
› Offer "EU/SG-hosted private inference" as a $99/mo tier — same model, different region.

Steal this: a dashboard that compares $/hour and $/token across Zankore, NEXTDC, Crusoe, and CoreWeave so founders cut inference costs by 30%.

3️⃣
India — Application layer still eats 90% of funding

What's happening:

› Nvidia has joined the India Deep Tech Alliance as new members added over $850M in capital commitments.
› Qualcomm Ventures, InfoEdge Ventures, Chiratae and Kalaari are among the new investors backing deep-tech.
› Nearly 90% of AI funding in India has gone into application-layer companies versus 85% to infra in the US.

What it means for you:

› Don't build infra for India — build a vertical workflow that sits on top of this new alliance-funded compute.
› TCS unit HyperVault is putting up to $7.4B for a 1GW campus for hyperscalers — you can resell India-hosted private AI to EU buyers.
› Launch a lite $19/mo version in India for one use case — tender drafting, GST filing, clinic notes — get 20 logos, use them as proof in US/EU.

Seeing a political movement as a threat isn’t automatically racism. And calling every Zionist a “white supremacist” is the lazy version of an argument.

Ask the less comfortable, more boring question: Why do millions of people leave Middle Eastern states seeking asylum, while virtually no one is fleeing Europe, America, or Australia to seek refuge in those same states?

Is Israel the explanation? Israel has roughly two million Arab citizens who vote, hold political office, and participate in its public institutions. Whatever your criticism of Israel, reducing the entire issue to “white supremacy” explains very little.

People generally don’t flee to Damascus, Sana’a, or Baghdad in search of liberal rights and accountable government. They flee systems they believe offer them fewer freedoms, fewer opportunities, or less security.

And Zionism is not the same thing as Great Replacement Theory. Zionism is a nationalist movement centered on Jewish self-determination and the establishment and preservation of a Jewish state in the historic homeland of the Jewish people.

If the claim is that Israel “cannot exist,” then make the argument precisely: Why is a state with competitive elections, independent courts, and millions of Arab citizens uniquely illegitimate, while the authoritarian systems across the region that have produced enormous refugee flows are often treated as secondary to the discussion?

Criticize Israel all you want. But labels aren’t arguments. If you’re going to call an entire political movement “white supremacist,” explain the standard you’re applying and apply it consistently.

text:
I genuinely think that what college sports needs right now is some appellate architecture to these nonsensical, sweeping TROs and injunctions. The Baton Rouge PI actually requires the SEC to obtain leave of a Louisiana state court before it may declare any of the 32 plaintiffs ineligible. Right. A private association must file a motion and ask a trial judge's permission before applying its own bylaws. And the order does not stop with the plaintiffs. It bars enforcement of any SEC rule or proposed penalty against any institution the plaintiffs choose to play for and against any institution that plays them, which is to say most of Division I. One judge in Baton Rouge has made himself the eligibility commissioner of college athletics. Ridiculous.

But the way to fix that is through the Louisiana appellate system. Supervisory writs exist for exactly this, and if this injunction is as indefensible as I think it is, it will not survive review. That's the ordinary, unglamorous, correct path for a litigant who believes a state trial court has overreached. Appear, lose, take writs, go up. The SEC appeared. Sankey testified. The SEC lost. But instead of going up it went sideways to a federal courthouse in Birmingham, against a football coach, an athletic director, a university president, 15 board members about whom its complaint alleges precisely nothing, and an AG who by the SEC's own admissions has done nothing but offer what is truly a pathetic, god-awful amicus brief.

And I still don't see the First Amendment problem. Nobody is forcing this association. The conference admitted LSU, retains LSU, and holds the power to expel LSU by a 2/3rds vote of its presidents. It has now noticed that very meeting. What the SEC is really asking for is an advisory opinion blessing a vote it is already free to take. Federal courts do not issue those. But, to be clear, it doesn't need one. If the SEC believes LSU has lost institutional control and that its continued membership is incompatible with the conference's values, give LSU the boot and defend that decision wherever it is challenged.

Nor do I see the irreparable injury. No professional athlete has played a down in an SEC game. LSU rostered nobody. The harm the SEC identifies is that its own meeting might be delayed by people who have not moved to delay it, and delay is the definition of reparable harm. You reconvene. Worse, the SEC noticed the September 10 meeting at the same moment it asked for emergency relief to protect the September 10 meeting. You cannot set the fuse and then complain about how short it is.

So: an association free to act, asking a court for permission it does not need, on an emergency it created, against defendants who cannot give it the one thing it actually wants. Meanwhile the order that is genuinely doing the damage sits unchallenged in Baton Rouge. 

Which is why I am watching the Tenth Circuit in Winse. Somebody has to say what the limits are, and it is not going to be the trial courts.
