text:
Zee looks at him. NuNew looks back.
Finally, Zee sighs and asks, “Why are you looking for it?”

“To find the Book of Death.”

The rope slips from Zee’s hand. For a moment, he simply looks at NuNew like he has lost his mind.

“You’re looking for what?”

“The Book of Death.”

Zee passes a hand over his face. “What possible reason could an academy student have for wanting that tome?”

NuNew’s grip tightens around the map. “Haven’t you heard what’s happening?”

“I might have.”

“Then you must be aware that a necromancer is raising an army. People are dying. That tome contains a spell that could stop him.”

“And the academy sent you?”

NuNew folds the map. “I didn’t say that.”

Zee looks at him again in disbelief. 

“The point is that someone needs to find it.”

“So you volunteered?”

“More or less.”

“And what makes you think you can get anywhere near it?”

NuNew hesitates. Then he lifts his sleeve enough to reveal the crest over his wrist. The mark catches the afternoon light. Zee’s eyes drop to it. Whatever response NuNew expects, it is not the sudden silence.

Then Zee looks back at his face. “Holy shit.”

NuNew raises an eyebrow.

“You’re the pearl mage.”

“Yes.”

Zee looks towards the tree. Then back at NuNew. Then he starts laughing.

NuNew folds his arms. “What is so funny?”

“You. Attempting to reach the most heavily protected tomb in the kingdom by yourself.”

“It’s a temple.”

“It will become your tomb because you’ll die inside it.”

“I’m not going to die.”

“Thats debatable.”

“I would appreciate a little help.”

“I helped. You’re no longer hanging from a tree.”

“I need help with directions, please.”

“Sure. Take that road and it will lead you back to the academy.”

NuNew draws himself up. “I’m not going back.”

“Then find somewhere with wards and competent mages.”

“And wait for someone else to solve everything?”

“Yes. Ideally.” The words sting more than NuNew wants them to.

“Thank you for getting me down.” He bends to collect the last of his belongings. “I’ll find a way myself.”

Zee watches him and then sighs. “Reaching Lux alone would be suicide.”

NuNew stills. There it was again. That certainty in the hunter’s voice which makes Nunew certain that he knows more than he lets on.

“You know where it is.”

“I know enough to stay away from it.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

Zee says nothing.

“Do you know how to find it?”

A breeze moves through the branches above them. Finally, Zee answers.

“Yes.”

For the first time since opening his ancestor’s letter, this mission did not feel completely hopeless.

“Show me.”

“No.”

“You just said…”

“I said I knew how. I didn’t offer to take you.”

“How do you know?”

Zee stops to retrieve the fallen rope. “Someone entrusted me with a map.”

“Who?”

“Someone who told me not to use it unless there is a good reason.”

“An army of the dead seems like a very good reason.”

“I’m aware.”

“Then why haven’t you gone?”

Zee finishes winding the rope with unnecessary care. “The map has not been particularly cooperative.”

NuNew frowns. “What does that mean?”

“It means I don’t wanna talk about it.”

“Fine. Then tell me why did he give it to you?”

“He trusted me.”

“I’ve known you for less than an hour and already find that difficult to believe.”

“The feeling is mutual.”

Zee begins gathering the rest of his equipment. NuNew follows him around.

“The letter I found says the route was known to a shadow mage. If this person had the map, he might have known someone from the House of Black.”

“He’s dead.”

NuNew stops. The answer leaves no room for another question, but he asks one anyway.

“Did he tell you anything about them?”

Zee tightens a strap on his pack.

“He told me to keep the map safe.”

NuNew studies him. He cannot tell whether Zee is grieving, concealing something or simply determined to make every answer as unhelpful as possible.

“I need to see it.”

Zee doesn’t answer him and continues to collect his things +

text:
At the time of this interview, Warren Buffett was 57 years old with a net worth of approximately $2.1 billion.

The interviewer poses a clear question: if someone had invested $10,000 with Buffett back in 1956, what would that investment be worth today?

Buffett responds: slightly over $15 million.

He then spends the next twenty minutes clarifying the reasoning behind that figure.

His method for valuing investments starts with a basic analogy: a bond clearly states its future payments, but a business does not. As an investor, your task is to project those future "coupons" on your own.

Buffett shares insights from some of his most successful investments, such as The Washington Post, which was valued at around $80 million when he believed its real worth was at least $400 million, along with GEICO and See’s Candies.

However, the key lesson is patience.

He emphasizes that even if the stock market were to close for two years, it wouldn't matter as long as the companies you hold continue to increase in value.

Just a few months after the 1987 crash, he also offers timeless advice: structure your life in a way that, even in the face of extraordinary events, you remain capable of moving forward and playing your part the next day.

Buffett explains how speculative financial tools can create opportunities for disciplined investors. When such instruments cause irrational behavior, they can eventually lead to unjustified prices.

There are no complex models or market forecasts involved.

The key is to understand the business, estimate its true worth, maintain control over your emotions, and then patiently wait.

Despite being nearly four decades old, this interview still feels surprisingly relevant and current.

text:
The "segregation forever" governor spent his final years asking Vivian Malone to forgive him. George Wallace had once put his own body in a schoolhouse door to keep her out of college. In 1996, frail and in a wheelchair, he told her to her face that it had been wrong, that it never should have happened.

At the end, he was the one who needed something from her.

A wiry man stood in a doorway with his hands behind his back. He was the governor of Alabama, and his whole body was the answer to a 20-year-old woman who had only come to register for summer classes.

The doorway belonged to Foster Auditorium at the University of Alabama.

The date was June 11, 1963, and the woman's name was Vivian Malone.

She had grown up in Mobile, the oldest of eight children. Both her parents worked at Brookley Air Force Base, her father in maintenance and her mother as a domestic, and in their house college was simply something you were going to do.

She had been a student at Alabama A&M, a Black college up in Huntsville. It did not offer the business courses she wanted, so she applied to the white university in Tuscaloosa, and when they refused her, she took them to court and won her place as a junior.

There was a quiet way to do a thing like this. There was always a side entrance, a back hallway, a version where a Black student slipped in, kept her head down, and made sure nobody had to look at her.

Vivian Malone did not want that version.

"My goal was to go to the University of Alabama, and I didn't feel that I should sneak in," she said years later. "I didn't feel that I should have to go around the back door."

"If he was standing in the door, I had every right in the world to face him and to go to school."

Before any door, before the cameras, two men had come to her family's home in Mobile. They were white, and they brought a warning, that threats had been made against her, and that the law would not be able to keep her safe.

Her parents heard all of it. Eight children, a maintenance paycheck, a domestic's wages, and a daughter who wanted to walk into a school that did not want her inside it.

She went anyway.

The morning of June 11 was already hot when the federal marshals drove her in toward Tuscaloosa. She would carry the small, strange details of that ride for the rest of her life.

The drink machines on campus had been emptied out. Someone had decided that full bottles were a hazard, that a crowd holding Coca-Colas could turn those bottles into something to throw.

State troopers stood in a ring around Foster Auditorium.

The governor had a podium waiting at the door, with microphones, because the entire purpose of the morning was to be seen refusing.

Vivian and James Hood, the other Black student admitted that day, did not walk up to the door.

They waited in a car.

A man named Nicholas Katzenbach, the deputy attorney general of the United States, walked up in their place. He asked Governor Wallace to step aside and let the students through.

Wallace did not move. He read out a prepared statement about the rights of a sovereign state, calling the federal presence an illegal seizure of power, and he refused to budge.

So the students were taken to their dormitory rooms, and the country sat and waited. In Washington, President Kennedy signed the order that placed the Alabama National Guard under federal command, lifting it clean out of Wallace's hands.

That afternoon, a Guard general named Henry Graham walked up to the same door. He was in uniform, federalized now, and he told the governor it was his sad duty to ask him to step aside.

Wallace read a second statement.

Then he left.

Vivian Malone walked into Foster Auditorium and registered for her classes. After the troopers and the emptied machines and the man in the door, the thing itself came down to paperwork on a table.

She told the reporters outside that she was glad it was finished, and that she had come for one thing only, an education.

She would not perform for them.

She explained the choice plainly later. "I took myself out of the role of being maybe some kind of heroine or some kind of special person," she said.

"I just said, I am here. I'm a student, and I'm going to be a student."

In her own mind she had braced for something close to an ordinary day. "I expected it to go pretty smoothly," she said.

"Of course, I don't think the system was ready for me at that time, but I was ready for them."

That same evening, President Kennedy went on television and told the country that this was, at its root, a moral question. He called it one as old as scripture and as plain as the nation's founding promises, and the day a young woman signed up for business classes in Alabama became the day a president finally said it out loud.

A few hours later, in Mississippi, a man named Medgar Evers pulled into his own driveway and lost his life there. That was the shape of that single week, a door forced open in Tuscaloosa and a leader taken in Jackson, inside the same few hours.

James Hood did not last long in Tuscaloosa. The weight on him was real and the threats around him were real, and within roughly two months he was gone, off to finish his studies somewhere that was not trying to break him.

No one should hold his leaving against him.

But it left Vivian Malone as the only one.

She was the lone Black face in her classrooms. She carried her tray into a cafeteria where every open seat was a small decision, and she studied in a dormitory the rest of the campus could point to by name.

There were no easy late-night friendships waiting down the hall, no soft landing, no version of these years where she got to just be a young woman figuring out her twenties. She had handed all of that away the moment she refused the back door.

In November of 1963, three bombs went off near the campus. One of them was four blocks from her dormitory.

She could have packed a bag that night. Anyone alive would have understood it.

"I decided not to show any fear and went to classes that day," she said.

Then she did it again the next morning, and the morning after that.

She finished.

In 1965, Vivian Malone became the first Black student ever to graduate from the University of Alabama, two years after its governor stood in the school's door to keep her out.

There is a small human grace in how she got to class each day. The university had hired a young man from nearby Stillman College to be her driver, a student named Mack Jones.

She married him.

He went on to become an obstetrician, a man whose whole working life was spent bringing babies safely into the world.

After she graduated, Vivian Malone went to work for the Civil Rights Division of the United States Department of Justice, the same federal government that had needed marshals and the National Guard to walk her through one doorway. Later she directed environmental justice work at the EPA.

The young woman who had been told she could not take business courses spent the rest of her career inside that government, enforcing the laws that were supposed to protect people like her.

In 1996, she saw George Wallace again. He had asked to see her.

He was an old man in a wheelchair by then, his voice gone soft and raspy, his hearing nearly gone. They met at the Alabama state capitol, the same building where Jefferson Davis was once sworn in as president of the Confederacy, the same place where Wallace had once promised segregation forever.

His family had created an award for courage, and they handed the very first one to her, the woman he had once tried to stop at a door.

She did not pretend the years away. She asked him the question to his face.

"I asked him why did he do it," she said.

"He said he did what he felt needed to be done at that point in time, but he would not do that today. At that point, we spoke, I spoke, of forgiveness."

She had told people for years where her steadiness came from. "I was never afraid," she said.

"God was with me."

Vivian Malone Jones died in 2005, at 63, after a stroke. She did not live to see what her old university would finally do with that doorway.

In 2010, the school dedicated the ground outside Foster Auditorium as the Malone-Hood Plaza, anchored by a clock tower named for Autherine Lucy, the first Black student it had ever admitted. James Hood lived to stand for that one, the man who had left and come back to earn his own doctorate there in 1997.

The door where a governor once stood became a place that carries her name.

Her children stood in for her that day, and so did her sister Sharon, who arrived alongside her husband, Eric Holder, the Attorney General of the United States.

The federal government had once been forced to fight its way to that doorway just to walk Vivian Malone through it. Now the man running its Justice Department stood in the plaza named for her, because by then he was family.

She had said once, back when nobody was sure she would even make it through, what she believed she was doing there. "I see myself as being part of that change where doors could be opened for generations to come," she told an interviewer.

The doorway still stands in Tuscaloosa, under the tower and the markers with her name. Students pass it on their way to class every day, most of them carrying nothing heavier than a backpack, which is the whole of what she walked in there to make possible.

🇺🇲 Andrew & Tristan Tate will remain in a Miami detention center after a federal judge denied their request for bail while they fight extradition to the U.K.

The brothers were arrested in July and are wanted in Britain over a total of 59 criminal charges, including rape and human trafficking for sexual exploitation.

Both deny the allegations. Prosecutors argued they are a flight risk and pose a danger, pointing to their wealth, multiple passports and access to private jets and boats.

Their lawyers offered to surrender their passports, accept GPS monitoring and undergo home inspections, but Magistrate Judge Lauren F. Louis ruled that they had not shown the "special circumstances" required for bail in an international extradition case.

The U.K. is expected to submit its formal extradition request to the U.S. by September 16.

A U.S. court will then consider whether the legal requirements for extradition are met. If extradition is certified, the brothers can challenge the decision through judicial review and appeals, potentially extending the case for years.

These are a few thing DJT has done for others that doesn’t get much media coverage:

Trump’s Good Deeds

Weird how you never hear about any of this in the news...... TRUMP DOES THE UNTHINKABLE...
I've never heard anything negative about the man until he announced he was running for president.
• He's never even tried alcohol or tobacco. He doesn't do drugs. 
• His work ethic is beyond unparalleled as a hardworking businessman. 
• He's one of the most generous celebrities in the world with a heart filled with more gold than his $100 million New York penthouse.

Since the media has failed so miserably at reporting the truth about Trump, I decided to put together some of the acts of kindness he's committed over three decades which has gone virtually unnoticed or fallen on deaf ears. 

• In 1986, Trump prevented the foreclosure of Annabell Hill's family farm after her husband committed suicide. Trump personally phoned down to the auction to stop the sale of her home and offered the widow money. Trump decided to take action after he saw Hill's pleas for help in news reports. 
• In 1988, a commercial airline refused to fly Andrew Ten, a sick Orthodox Jewish child with a rare illness. The boy had to travel with an elaborate life-support system. Trump contacted the grief-stricken parents after hearing this and didn't hesitate to send his own plane to take the child from Los Angeles to New York so he could get his treatment. 
• In 1991, 200 Marines who served in Operation Desert Storm spent time at Camp Lejune in North Carolina before they were scheduled to return home to their families. However, the Marines were told that a mistake had been made and an aircraft would not be able to take them home on their scheduled departure date. When Trump got wind of this, he sent his plane to make two trips from North Carolina to Miami to safely return the Gulf War Marines to their loved ones. 
• In 1995, a motorist stopped to help Trump after the limo he was traveling in got a flat tire. Trump asked the Good Samaritan how he could repay him for his help. All the man asked for was a bouquet of flowers for his wife. A few weeks later Trump sent the flowers with a note that read: We've paid off your mortgage. 
• In 1996, Trump filed a lawsuit against the city of Palm Beach , Florida, accusing the town of discriminating against his Mar-a-Lago resort club because it allowed Jews and blacks. Abraham Foxman, who as the Anti-Defamation League Director at the time, said Trump put the light on Palm Beach not on the beauty and the glitter, but on its seamier side of discrimination. Foxman also noted that Trump's charge had a trickle-down effect because other clubs followed his lead and began admitting Jews and blacks. 
• In 2000, Maury Povich featured a little girl named Megan who struggled with Brittle Bone Disease on his show and Trump happened to be watching. Trump said the little girl's story and positive attitude touched his heart. So he contacted Maury and gifted the little girl and her family with a very generous check. 
• In 2008, after Jennifer Hudson's family members were tragically murdered in Chicago , Trump put the Oscar-winning actress and her family up at his Windy City hotel for free. In addition to that, Trump's security took extra measures to ensure Hudson and her family members were safe during such a difficult time. 
• In 2013, New York bus driver Darnell Barton spotted a woman close to the edge of a bridge staring at the traffic below as he drove by. He stopped the bus, got out and put his arm around the woman and saved her life by convincing her to not jump. When Trump heard about this story, he sent the hero bus driver a check simply because he believed his good deed deserved to be rewarded. 
• In 2014, Trump gave $25,000 to Sgt. Andrew Tamoressi after he spent seven months in a Mexican jail for accidentally crossing the US-Mexico border. President Barack Obama couldn't even be bothered to make one phone call to assist with

Republicans Blow the Lid off “Birth Tourism” Epidemic
A Miami doctor whose "Have My Baby in Miami" site claimed 2,000 deliveries took the Fifth when Congress asked about Chinese officials and MS-13 members using birth tourism to secure citizenship for their children.
By Sarah Katherine Sisk
Contributing Writer
September 9, 2026
·
5 min read
Listen · 6 min
AMAC Radio

A Miami doctor who runs a business called “Have My Baby in Miami” repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment last week when Congress questioned his involvement in a scheme to help foreign nationals give birth in the United States for the purpose of obtaining American citizenship for their children.
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-TX) questioned Dr. Wladimir Lorentz, the founder and chief medical officer of Miami Medical Concierge Services, which does business as “Have My Baby in Miami,” at a House Oversight Committee hearing on birth tourism. Lorentz replied that a truthful answer could incriminate him.

Gill then displayed the company’s website, which advertised maternity services for international patients and claimed more than 2,000 international deliveries. One line on Have My Baby in Miami’s public website stated, “Now, the dream of having a child in the United States is closer to reality than you ever imagined.” It offered a step-by-step guide for parents traveling to Miami for childbirth, as well as help with housing and legal consultations.
AMAC Magazine, free with membership
Gill asked why the company modified or removed the site after the committee began investigating in May. He also asked whether Lorentz’s business had helped members of the Chinese Communist Party obtain U.S. citizenship for their children or facilitated childbirth for members of narco-terrorist organizations, including Tren de Aragua and MS-13. Lorentz invoked the Fifth Amendment each time.
“Birth tourism” is the practice of exploiting American citizenship by treating it as a commodity that can be bought and sold. A family hires a company, like Lorentz’s, to arrange medical appointments, temporary living arrangements, international insurance, and other paperwork. The mother gives birth here. Having obtained citizenship for her child, she then returns home to raise her child abroad.
In May, the House Oversight Committee requested the company’s marketing materials, service agreements, visa-related documents, and other guidance for clients applying at U.S. embassies or arriving at the border.
This is not the first instance of potential birth-tourism related crimes. In 2024, a California jury convicted Michael Wei Yueh Liu and Jing Dong of operating a birth-tourism scheme that charged Chinese clients tens of thousands of dollars to give birth in the United States and secure birthright citizenship for their children.

The pair were convicted of conspiracy and international money laundering. Prosecutors said they coached clients to hide their pregnancies and their plans to give birth in the United States from visa officials.

A foreign national may technically give birth in the United States, but the State Department can deny a visitor visa to an applicant traveling principally to give birth here so her child receives U.S. citizenship. An applicant who hides that purpose to obtain a visa may face charges of fraud or material misrepresentation.

Birth tourism is a massive national-security threat. The children born through these arrangements often grow up overseas, with little connection to the United States. Yet they can enter the United States without first obtaining a visa, work in most jobs, receive public benefits, and, as citizens, qualify to seek a security clearance.

The hypothetical scenarios are alarming. A Chinese Communist Party member could give birth in the United States, raise that baby in China, and then the child could return to the United States to vote in American elections or even run for office.

he had spent decades splitting his life between two completely different worlds studying baboon troops alone in the kenyan bush for months at a time and then coming back to teach some of the smartest 19 year olds in the country neuroscience genetics and evolution in the same breath

twenty five lectures got filmed that spring semester meant only for stanford's own students and years later people with no biology background at all started watching the entire course start to finish on their own because a man who spent his summers living with wild primates turned out to be one of the clearest teachers most of them had ever heard

text:
Thomas Edward “T. E.” Lawrence (b. 16 August 1888) was born in Tremadog, Wales, the son of Sir Thomas Chapman, an Anglo-Irish landowner, and Sarah Junner, a governess to the Chapman’s daughters. Chapman left his wife and family to live with Sarah. Unable to marry, the couple assumed the surname “Lawrence,” and their five sons (T. E. was the 2nd born) were illegitimate — a fact carefully concealed during Lawrence’s youth and one he remained sensitive about as an adult. His mother Sarah was herself illegitimate.

Lawrence entered Jesus College, Oxford, in 1907. Fascinated by medieval history and archaeology, he earned first-class honors after researching Crusader castles in France and the Middle East — cycling 2,200 miles through France to the Mediterranean and back in the summer of 1908, and in the summer of 1909, travelling 1,000 miles on foot while doing a three-month walking tour of Ottoman Syria.

During the Arab Revolt of 1916–18, Lawrence served as a British intelligence officer and liaison to Arab forces fighting the Ottoman Empire. Working closely with Prince Faisal, Lawrence helped organize guerrilla operations and the celebrated capture of Aqaba in 1917. To the British public desperately in need of heroes after the devastating and largely futile pyrrhic victory of WWI, his courage, theatrical appearance in Arab dress, and later publicity (much of it exaggerated or outright invented by the American writer Lowell Thomas), transformed the relatively small (5’5”), intensely private T. E. into the legendary “Lawrence of Arabia.” He later recounted his experiences in the Arab revolt against the Turks in the psychologically revealing memoir, Seven Pillars of Wisdom (1926).

Lawrence never married, and there is no conclusive evidence that he had a conventional sexual relationship with either a woman or man. In 1992, the London Daily Telegraph uncovered evidence which strongly suggested Lawrence was actively gay. His writings also reveal powerful emotional attachments to men, particularly the young Syrian Dahoum, nicknamed Sheik Ahmed, with whom he shared his quarters for three years, and to whom Seven Pillars was dedicated.

In Seven Pillars he acknowledged (and I quote) that the soldiers, rather than use the "sordid commerce" of public prostitutes "began indifferently to slake one another's few needs in their own clean bodies – a cold convenience that, by comparison, seemed sexless and even pure. Later, some began to justify this sterile process, and swore that friends quivering together in the yielding sand with intimate hot limbs in supreme embrace, found there hidden in the darkness a sensual co-efficient of the mental passion which was welding OUR [my emphasis] souls and spirits in one flaming effort." Whew! He went on to say that "Several, thirsting to punish appetites they could not wholly prevent, took a savage pride in degrading the body, and offered themselves fiercely in any habit which promised physical pain or filth."

Okay, then. I’m not a psychiatrist, but even I can figure out that the passages cited above, and the use of the word “our” describing the sexual activities of his fellow soldiers (and obviously himself) strongly suggest a closeted homosexual who was so wracked with guilt over his base needs, that he turned to masochism and regular whippings (which commenced until he achieved sexual release) as a necessary form of punishment. In fact, years after Lawrence’s death, John Bruce, a fellow Scotsman and soldier, revealed that he had been hired by T. E. to regularly administer severe, ritualistic floggings.

Although Lawrence’s sexuality continues to be debated by historians and biographers, what is clearer is that he moved comfortably within a remarkable circle of homosexual British literary and artistic men — most notably E. M. Forster, Noel Coward, Siegfried Sassoon, the immensely wealthy Sir Philip Sassoon (Siegfried’s cousin) at whose lavish estates he frequently stayed, and Robert Graves (his early biographer).

Haunted by fame, Lawrence sought anonymity in the Royal Air Force under assumed names. He retired from the RAF in February 1935, hoping finally to live austerely at his simple home Clouds Hill. He enjoyed that freedom for only a few months. On 13 May 1935, while riding his motorcycle near the cottage, he swerved to avoid two boys on bicycles and was thrown from the machine. He suffered severe head injuries and died seven days later at age 46. He was buried at Moreton, Dorset in a plain elm coffin, wrapped in a Union Jack, with no flowers or official military displays.

Behind the romantic legend was a far more elusive, complicated man — brilliant, physically daring, emotionally guarded and deeply uncomfortable with fame. His illegitimate birth, ambiguous sexuality, intense male friendships, identification with Arab companions, and later flight into anonymity all contributed to the making of T. E. Lawrence — one of the most complex British figures of the 20th century. 🏳️‍🌈

I was invited onto @1DimeOfficial's podcast for a long-ranging discussion about the topics I’ve been studying over the past few years and relate to my book project on Mathew and Henry Carey. We explored the forgotten tradition of political economy that refuses the usual choice between Marxism and free-market liberalism. We contrast Karl Marx with Friedrich List and Matthew and Henry Carey, trace economic nationalism from the American System to MMT and Ha-Joon Chang, and ask whether national sovereignty, protectionism, and state capacity offer a more practical path to development and anti-imperialism. In Tony’s Patreon-exclusive segments, we expand this conversation across three additional episodes. We discuss nationalist internationalism and Arnold Toynbee’s theory of civilizational cycles; Henry Carey, rentierism, Marxism, and the Irish struggle for national liberation; and, in a nearly three-hour finale, the post-left/post-right convergence, the moral limits of markets, immigration, industrial policy, class coalitions, empire, and whether any populist project can escape establishment capture.

text:
VISA $V IS THE CREDIT REFERENCE FOR CRYPTO CARDS THAT OWE IT MONEY:

Visa V at $367.63, -$1.02 / -0.28% today. The San Francisco company runs the network that takes a small cut whenever a card is tapped. It issues no cards and lends nobody money.

Second place on a list is behind for one specific, nameable reason. Find the reason and you learn something the winner's write-up never teaches. Six names below, one per Len5, each with the single thing holding it a notch short. Visa's is the price, and nothing else.

Start with a gap nobody thinks about. When you tap a card, Visa does not wait for your bank to collect from you. The card program on the other side owes Visa its settlement money on Visa's schedule, cash collected or not. A large American bank covers that in its sleep. A crypto card start-up has to hold spare cash or borrow to bridge the days in between.

On Tuesday, September 8, Visa opened its own settlement data to lenders operating on blockchains, so they can finance exactly that gap for stablecoin card programs - stablecoins being digital tokens designed to hold a fixed value, usually one US dollar. Through a platform called Credit Coop, an issuer gets a credit line covering what it owes Visa, drawn and repaid automatically as customer payments arrive. Credit Coop has financed more than $2.5B since 2023 across 3,000+ borrowings, no defaults.

Visa sized the corner this touches: 160+ stablecoin-linked card programs on its network, payment volume on them up close to 200% in a year, and its own stablecoin settlement volume past a $20B annualized run rate, more than fifteen times a year ago. Fifteen-fold is a real growth rate; $20B is a small number. Settlement volume is what Visa moves with its banks, not what shoppers spend - but the sizes place it. $20B a year, beside more than $4 trillion of card spending in one quarter.

Then this morning at 5:34am ET, the same problem with no blockchain in it. The International Finance Corporation, the private-sector arm of the World Bank Group, will share the credit settlement risk on Visa transactions at enrolled banks - about $200M of risk sharing over five years, starting with 14 Latin American and Caribbean countries and roughly 50 institutions rated below investment grade, meaning lenders judge them likelier than average to miss a payment. Visa wants those banks issuing cards. It does not want to carry the risk one of them cannot settle.

The business funding it, reported July 28 for the three months to June 30:

- Net revenue $11.6B, +14%
- Adjusted profit, meaning earnings with certain costs stripped out, $3.32 a share, +11%
- Payments volume past $4 trillion in one quarter for the first time, +10% once currency swings are stripped out
- Processed transactions 71.7B, +10%; cross-border volume +13%; $6.2B returned to owners

Quality-Value wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, at a price short of its worth, and Visa is its runner-up on the second half alone. Rebuilding a network 71.7 billion transactions deep is not the argument. The price is: about 32 times the last year of reported profit, or 28 times if the next three quarters merely match the $3.32 just earned, and 4.7% under the $385.57 it reached on August 26. CHANGE IT: that 10%. While card taps compound near it, everything above is a rounding error. The test comes if taps slow while a settlement rail arrives that needs no card at all - and on September 1 a group of 21 financial institutions announced plans for a bank-issued dollar stablecoin targeting the first half of 2027. WHEN: the financial year ends September 30, the fourth-quarter report is not company-dated, and calendars point to about October 27.

MOMENTUM LEN5:
- Nurix Therapeutics, ticker NRIX, at $26.20, +$0.07 / +0.27% today, 7.2% under the $28.23 of August 19. The Brisbane, California company designs pills that make a diseased cell destroy its own harmful proteins. This style wants the recent stretch of a climb and the longer one agreeing near a high; only the six-month leg still does, the past month having gone flat. The climb came with a receipt: its Roche partnership on bexobrutideg, its lead blood-cancer drug, closed July 21 with $700M of cash up front and up to $2.3B if milestones land. Cash was $443.5M at May 31; with that payment it is near $1.14B against a company worth $2.72B, so two fifths of the price is money already in the bank. WATCH: the quarter ended August 31, calendars point to early October - the first accounts to show the $700M. RISK: it loses money, and one partner carries the case. VERDICT: the cheque cleared and the climb stopped.

DEEP-VALUE & SPECIAL-SITUATIONS LEN5:
- Gartner, ticker IT, at $168.89, -$3.70 / -2.14% today, after Tuesday took another 7.4% off it. The Stamford, Connecticut company sells research subscriptions to technology and business leaders. This style wants a good business marked down after something visible and dated, and the dated thing is a document Gartner wrote about itself: a September 1 survey of 1,303 executives found only 22% had scaled artificial intelligence beyond one part of their business. Buyers read that as software beating advice. August 4 argued back - adjusted profit $4.37 a share, +24%; $547M spent on its own shares in three months; contract value, meaning subscription dollars already signed, $5.3B, growing faster for a second straight quarter and at 3.3% with the US federal government set aside; the year raised to at least $14.00 of profit, about 12 times today's price and 36.5% under the $265.85 of last September. What holds it short: the discount only pays if Gartner wins an argument about artificial intelligence, and the sharpest evidence against it is Gartner's own research. WATCH: that $5.3B going backwards, early November. VERDICT: the cheapest name here, marked down by a number it published itself.

GROWTH LEN5:
- BOK Financial, ticker BOKF, at $134.90, -$0.83 / -0.61% today, 8.1% under the $146.84 of August 17. The Tulsa bank lends across eight states and runs a wealth arm beside it. This style wants real profit growth the price has not already charged for. Not charged for is settled at about 12.8 times profit and 1.36 times book value - roughly what would be left after selling up and paying everyone off. Growing runs straight back to the top of this post. The June quarter earned $176.5M, or $2.92 a share, but $30.9M of that before tax was a one-off gain from exchanging its Visa shares under Visa's own exchange offer; strip that and a bond-portfolio loss and it is $2.59. About eleven cents of every reported dollar of profit was Visa's. What repeats is better: loans hit $27.1B, up $896M / +3.4% in three months, and the full-year loan growth map was raised above 10%. What holds it short: a third of revenue is fees, answering to mortgage rates nobody in Tulsa sets. WATCH: loan growth under that 10% floor, around October 19-20. VERDICT: the lending was its own work; a slice of the headline profit was not.

HYPERGROWTH LEN5:
- AppLovin, ticker APP, at $306.36, -$5.65 / -1.81% today, only 3.0% above its own worst price of the past twelve months, $297.50 on August 24. The Palo Alto company decides which advertisement appears inside a phone app, with 898 employees. This style wants a business early as well as fast, and fast is not in dispute: for the three months to June 30, reported August 5, revenue $1.92B, +53%, with net income $1.27B - 66 cents of every sales dollar kept as profit. What holds it a notch short is a sentence from its own chief executive. Adam Foroughi told owners the quarter landed "just below the midpoint of our guidance range," cash profit under the range too, and added: "this quarter, we fell short of that standard." Missing a number you wrote yourself moves the argument from speed to duration, and the shares are down about 53% this year while that gets settled. WATCH: the $2.055B revenue floor management set for this quarter, early November. VERDICT: real growth, and the whole argument has moved to next year.

INCOME LEN5:
- Global Ship Lease, ticker GSL, at $45.02, +$0.31 / +0.68% today, 3.2% under the $46.50 of September 4. The Athens company owns containerships and rents them to shipping lines on long contracts, with seven people on the payroll. This style wants cash genuinely reaching owners and paid for by the business, and both halves are unusually clean here. Across the six months to June 30 it earned $180.7M on $396.8M of revenue - close to a million dollars of profit a day - with its ships in use 97.4% of the time. The cheque is $0.625 a quarter, $2.50 a year, about 5.6% of the price, and a quarter of the $2.48 the June quarter earned on its own. Nor is it hoping for freight rates: $3.2B of revenue is already contracted over an average remaining charter of 3.3 years. What holds it short: it has also committed $1.33B to 15 new ships for delivery from late 2028, real money against a company worth $1.62B. WATCH: new charters at rates that cover that order, early November. RISK: on August 26 the chief executive sold 30,000 shares and the finance chief 50,000, about $3.6M between them. VERDICT: the best-covered payment here, sitting beside the biggest bill.

Nothing Visa announced this week involved a card. Tuesday it taught blockchain lenders how to judge crypto card start-ups. This morning it got the World Bank's private arm to stand behind fifty banks rated below investment grade. Both are the same job: making sure the money owed to Visa turns up. A company working that hard on getting paid does not believe the payment is at risk - and at 28 times what it just earned, nobody buying the shares believes it either.

Not investment advice.

text:
I have had two of these engines.  The first came out of a death car Corvette that my girlfriend's brother and I installed in a 62 Vette, which also became a death car. The second was in a 1969 Camaro convertible.  Also a death car.  I doubt that back in the late 70s someone went to the trouble of cloning a Yenko Camaro. Heck, we are MoPar guys.  Who TF was Yenko anyway? "YSC" embroidered in the headrests?  I wanted it for my first car, and Papa Kriebs said "no way." I ended up with a clapped out '68 Barracuda 340-S convertible for $200 that burned/leaked 3 quarts of oil on the way to the shop which was all of six miles.  A story for another time.  Oh, and we fixed the Camaro and sold it for $8K to a guy in Jersey.  The next month it was in Hemmings for $27.5K
Fred Gibb ran a Chevrolet dealership in La Harpe, Illinois. Population under 1,500. A small-town dealer in a farming community who also happened to be an NHRA Super Stock drag racer. Gibb wanted the all-aluminum ZL-1 427 in a Camaro. Chevrolet wouldn't offer it. The ZL-1 was a racing engine, developed for the Can-Am series and the Corvette racing program. Aluminum block, aluminum heads, open-chamber cylinder heads with rectangular intake ports, forged steel crankshaft, forged steel rods, forged aluminum pistons. It weighed approximately 500 pounds, roughly the same as a small-block 350, despite displacing 427 cubic inches. Chevrolet built it for race cars, not for street cars. Gibb found the loophole.
The Central Office Production Order system, COPO, was GM's internal mechanism for fleet and specialty orders that fell outside the standard option catalog. Municipal vehicles, taxi cabs, ambulances, and other special-application orders were processed through COPO because they required non-standard equipment combinations. Vince Piggins, Chevrolet's performance products manager, had already used COPO 9560 to put the iron-block L72 427 into Camaros for 1969. Gibb and Piggins worked together to create COPO 9560 with the ZL-1 aluminum 427 instead of the iron L72. The order went through GM's system without corporate approval because the COPO process was designed for fleet orders that didn't require executive sign-off. An all-aluminum racing V8 in a production Camaro, approved by a clerical system designed for ordering taxicab packages.
The sticker price was absurd. The ZL-1 engine option added $4,160.15 to a base Camaro that cost approximately $3,300. The engine option cost more than the car underneath it. Total window sticker: approximately $7,200 to $7,800 depending on additional options. In 1969 dollars. A base Corvette cost $4,780. The ZL-1 Camaro cost nearly twice as much as the sports car it shared a corporate garage with. Gibb originally ordered 50 cars. Chevrolet eventually built 69 in total. Most sat on dealer lots unsold because nobody in rural Illinois or anywhere else was prepared to pay $7,500 for a Camaro. Gibb reportedly had to take many back and sell them at a loss.
Chevrolet rated the ZL-1 at 430 HP. The same number they stamped on the iron-block L72 427. The same number that had nothing to do with the engine's actual output and everything to do with keeping the published horsepower figure low enough that insurance companies wouldn't refuse to write policies. Independent dyno testing consistently showed the ZL-1 producing 570 to 580 HP in stock form. One hundred and forty horsepower more than advertised. The largest gap between rated and actual output of any production engine Chevrolet ever built. The L78 396 was underrated by 50 HP. The ZL-1 427 was underrated by 140. Chevrolet didn't lie by ten percent. They lied by thirty-three percent. On an engine that was already the most powerful thing the company had ever installed in a production car.
The ZL-1 ran 11.68 seconds at 122 mph in the quarter mile in stock trim on street tires with an automatic transmission. Faster than anything else on a dealer lot in 1969 from any manufacturer. The aluminum block shed nearly 100 pounds compared to the iron L72, which gave the ZL-1 Camaro an approximately 55/45 front-to-rear weight distribution instead of the nose-heavy 60/40 that iron big-block Camaros suffered. Less weight over the front wheels meant better weight transfer at launch, which meant better traction, which meant quicker elapsed times despite identical rated horsepower to the iron 427. The aluminum block was worth two tenths of a second in the quarter mile before any tuning. Chevrolet knew this. That is why the ZL-1 existed as a racing engine. The weight savings were not cosmetic. It was competitive.
Sixty-nine cars. An engine that cost more than the car. Rated at 430 HP, making 570. Ordered through a fleet paperwork system by a small-town dealer in Illinois. The ZL-1 Camaro is worth over $1 million today because sixty-nine exist, because the engine was underrated by 140 HP, and because a dealer in a town of 1,500 people exploited a loophole that GM's corporate structure never imagined anyone would find. The most powerful, most expensive, and most dishonestly rated production Chevrolet ever built exists because one man in La Harpe, Illinois, wanted to go drag racing and knew which form to fill out.

Another option that may be worth exploring for Colonel Anurag Upadhyay is the Shirley Ryan AbilityLab in Chicago, Illinois, particularly if his clinical condition is consistent with Locked-In Syndrome (LIS).

Shirley Ryan AbilityLab has a dedicated, specialized LIS rehabilitation program that has been running for nearly 20 years. The program was founded by Dr. Richard L. Harvey, a leading expert in stroke rehabilitation and LIS, and the team has treated nearly 100 patients with locked-in syndrome.

Their multidisciplinary approach includes respiratory management, swallowing and speech rehabilitation, eye care, communication technology, mobility and gait training, occupational therapy, and customized assistive technologies. Their published clinical experience also highlights cases where patients with LIS achieved meaningful improvements in communication, mobility, independence and quality of life.

I am not suggesting that this would necessarily be appropriate for Colonel Upadhyay, as that would require a detailed review of his medical records, neurological status, imaging and current functional abilities. However, given the complexity of LIS rehabilitation, seeking an expert evaluation or second opinion from a centre with this level of specialized experience could be worth considering.

Shirley Ryan AbilityLab also offers an expert second-opinion evaluation in which their physicians review medical records and develop an individualized assessment.

In a time when uncertainty shapes the national conversation, Saving America’s Citizens: Exercising Our Oath for Our Country by Tod Gohl emerges as both a reflection and a provocation. It is not just a story — it is a call to examine responsibility, patriotism, and the limits of leadership.

Blending memoir with speculative fiction, the book takes readers into the lived experiences of a U.S. Air Force veteran and extends them into a fictional yet unsettling vision of America’s future. Saving America’s Citizens: Exercising Our Oath for Our Country draws its strength from this duality — grounded in reality, yet bold enough to imagine what comes next.

The narrative paints a country on the brink. Violence escalates, societal order weakens, and trust in institutions begins to erode. The portrayal is intense, highlighting issues like crime, instability, and national security concerns, all contributing to a growing sense that the system is no longer working as intended.

At the center of it all is a powerful question: what happens when those sworn to protect a nation begin to believe that traditional systems — elections, leadership transitions, and policies — are no longer enough?

Rather than accepting decline, the protagonist takes a decisive turn. He forms a task force, driven by the same oath that once defined his service, to confront threats head-on. It is here that the story shifts from observation to action, exploring the moral and ethical weight of stepping beyond conventional boundaries in pursuit of national restoration.

What makes this book compelling is not just its premise, but its emotional undercurrent. There is a deep sense of frustration, but also hope — a belief that even in the darkest moments, there remains a path forward. The author channels his military background into a narrative that feels urgent, personal, and unapologetically bold.

For readers drawn to politically charged fiction, military insight, and stories that challenge the status quo, this book offers more than entertainment. It invites reflection. It asks difficult questions. And most importantly, it leaves you wondering where the line truly lies between duty and defiance.

In the end, Saving America’s Citizens is not about easy answers. It is about confronting uncomfortable realities — and daring to imagine what it would take to reclaim a nation’s future.

text:
Yes — Lindsay Clancy has admitted she killed her three children. That is not the same as a guilty plea to murder.
She is the former Massachusetts labor-and-delivery nurse charged in the January 24, 2023 deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months, in Duxbury. She pleaded not guilty to three counts of first-degree murder and put on an insanity / lack-of-criminal-responsibility defense (postpartum psychosis and related illness). The first trial ended in a mistrial on September 4, 2026 after a hung jury (reporting was 11–1 toward not guilty). A hearing is set for September 29. Prosecutors have not yet said whether they will retry her.
What counts as an admission

Her lawyers do not dispute that she caused the deaths. That was the defense position throughout the trial.
In a January 2026 medical-malpractice filing, she acknowledged she had killed the children.
Defense counsel later offered to stipulate in writing to her “involvement in the underlying conduct.” Prosecutors refused the stipulation and put on their own proof.
She later described the night to psychiatrists and other clinicians: a voice telling her to kill the children and herself, then the acts in the basement. Those accounts came in through expert testimony, not as a standalone recorded “I murdered them” cop-shop confession played as the state’s whole case.

What she said the night of
Patrick Clancy testified that when he found her outside she said “I tried to kill myself,” and that the children were in the basement. He did not describe her saying “I murdered them” in that moment. He later said she told him she had heard a voice.

If all the starting running backs in the Mid-Suburban League, or the entire Chicago area for that matter, got together for a group photo, Buffalo Grove High School's Matthew Kaput would stand out immediately. This is just a casual estimate, but the typical high school running back these days is maybe 5-foot-9 and super quick. There are a few exceptions. Kaput is completely beyond the ordinary. With a last name made for an XFL jersey, he stands 6-foot-3, dominates the offense for the 3-0 Bison, and also starts at linebacker. In fact, he excels at linebacker. His blitz and quarterback hit in the season opener against Hoffman Estates forced an interception and helped turn the game in Buffalo Grove's favor. When toting the rock, he's piled up 485 rushing yards in three games. “He's got to know a lot and he's a smart enough kid to handle it,” BG coach Jeff Vlk said. “He's kind of the whole package right now.” Buffalo Grove running back Matthew Kaput catches a pass during practice Tuesday in Buffalo Grove. (Joe Lewnard/Daily Herald) Buy Photo  To anyone watching a decent amount of high school games, Kaput's size at running back is almost alarming to see. From his perspective, he's just out there living his football life. “To be honest, I haven't really thought about it,” Kaput said. “I could see why people think it's unusual. “One of my favorite players in the NFL is Derrick Henry. I always loved watching him at Alabama when I was growing up, then at Tennessee and Baltimore. Still being as old as he is (32) and as big as he is (6-3, 252), usually you'd think they wouldn't last that long in the NFL. He's someone I looked up to.” Kaput may end up playing linebacker or tight end in college. He's got several FCS and Division II offers, with likely more on the way. But he's never wanted to give up the running back spot in high school. “Running back always felt like home to me,” he said. “I love to be in the trenches with the O-line, be able to find the hole and push for extra yards.” As a youth player for the Buffalo Grove Bills, he started out on the offensive line and spent a few years as the fullback in a Power-I offense, but he’s been carrying the ball ever since. He's also a third-year starter at running back. Buffalo Grove had a couple of thin classes the previous two years, so Kaput and the current senior group received heavy playing time since they were sophomores, which meant enduring 2-7 and 3-6 campaigns. “It was obviously tough not winning a lot of games those couple of seasons, but it really helped us grow,” he said. “It helped us get better at the game in general. We knew it was going to get better, especially with how hard we were working.” The payoff has arrived at Buffalo Grove, with three convincing wins to start the year and a battle of 3-0 teams coming up Thursday at Conant. “We've been very gritty in practice,” Kaput said. “This group really wants to win after these past two rough years. Our battles are mostly won up front, it seems. I wouldn't be anywhere without my line. They really push me for greatness.” And that last name could be an amazing marketing tool, especially for a linebacker. Per Merriam-Webster, kaput is defined as utterly finished, defeated or destroyed. All he knows is there was a great grandmother who emigrated from Germany and married a man named Kaput. “We don't really know the story behind it,” he said. No worries, just don't change a thing.

text:
I remember registration and licenses being so much easier in my home state of Oklahoma. I asked Grok to compare the two states. Keep in mind California has ~10X the amount of drivers as CA.
The two systems still feel like different philosophies of government, even after both states modernized.

Oklahoma kept a distributed contractor model. California kept a classic state bureaucracy and then bolted on partners, kiosks, and a huge online portal. Oklahoma’s local offices are the system. California’s field offices are the last resort.

Who actually runs the counter

Oklahoma. Service Oklahoma is the state agency. Most of the public-facing work happens at licensed operators—independent contractors who used to be called tag agents. They are not state employees. There are also about 31 state-run Service Oklahoma offices. Together they cover all 77 counties at roughly 270 locations. One small office often does both driver’s licenses and vehicle work.

California. The Department of Motor Vehicles is a large standalone state agency with about 8,300 employees. In-person licensing and testing happen at roughly 166–170 field offices staffed by state workers. Vehicle registration is split: the DMV itself, AAA branches (members only), thousands of authorized business partners, and self-service kiosks. Partners can charge extra service fees on top of state fees.

That is the core difference. In Oklahoma the “tag office” is the DMV for most people. In California the DMV is a state office, and private partners handle a slice of registration only.

Scale and density

California has about 28 million licensed drivers and 36 million registered vehicles. Oklahoma is an order of magnitude smaller. California therefore built fewer official offices relative to population and pushed routine work online. Oklahoma put a licensed operator in almost every county seat and many small towns, so physical access is denser even though the state is poorer and more rural.

California also has hundreds of DMV Now kiosks in grocery stores and similar spots for sticker renewals. Oklahoma’s equivalent is online Navigate plus walking into a tag agency.

Getting in the door

Oklahoma. Most licensed-operator offices are walk-in. Appointments are uncommon. After the February 2026 Navigate/BOOST cutover, standard in-person transactions were advertised as under 10 minutes. You often leave with a temporary printout; the card or plate arrives later.

California. Appointments dominate anything that still requires a field office: first license, REAL ID, out-of-state transfer, drive test, many title problems. Average appointment lead time is around two weeks statewide and much longer at busy urban offices. Walk-ins exist but can mean a long wait. The state has spent years pushing simple renewals out of offices so the remaining counters can handle identity work.

If you moved from Oklahoma to California, the cultural shock is not “there is a DMV.” It is “you cannot just drop in.”

What each counter can do

Oklahoma licensed operators are unusually broad: renew or replace a license or ID, REAL ID, many first-time licenses after tests, out-of-state transfers, titles, tags, plates, liens. Tests themselves are still limited to certain sites.

California field offices are the place for identity and testing. AAA and business partners do registration renewals, duplicate stickers, many title transfers, and plate orders—not licenses, not REAL ID, not drive tests. A Californian often uses three channels: website, AAA or a registration service, and a field office only when the law forces a face-to-face identity check.

Online

Both states now want you online first.

Oklahoma’s 2026 Navigate platform combined driver and vehicle records that used to live in separate systems. Renewals, address changes, and many registrations can be done there; you still pick a licensed operator if something physical has to be mailed.

California already offered more than 90 percent of transaction types online and completed tens of millions of digital transactions a year. Simple registration and eligible license renewals are supposed to stay out of field offices. California is also further along on a mobile driver’s license.

Rules that change the errand

A few legal differences matter more than the office names:

Plates. Oklahoma plates belong to the person and often move to the next car. California plates stay with the vehicle; most cars need front and rear plates. Oklahoma also pushed a 2024 pre-registration law so new purchases get metal plates quickly instead of lingering on paper tags.
Moving in. California requires a license transfer within 10 days of residency and still requires the written knowledge test; the road test is usually waived if you hold a valid U.S. license. Oklahoma tag agencies handle transfers more like any other license transaction.
Cost structure. Oklahoma registration is relatively flat and age-based; a 2026 law switched excise tax to actual sales price. California stacks a base fee, a value-based Vehicle License Fee, a Transportation Improvement Fee, and local sales tax with no trade-in credit on the tax. Registering an expensive car in California is a different bill.

What it feels like

Oklahoma still looks like the system you left: a storefront on Main Street, a contractor behind the counter, cash or card, same place for tags and licenses. The state added a modern backend and rebranded the agents, but the local network survived.

California looks like a large identity agency that does not want you in the building. The website and partners absorb volume. The field office is reserved for photos, documents, and tests—and you book it weeks ahead. That model scales to 40 million people. It is also why “the DMV” became a California punchline in a way Oklahoma’s tag agency never did.

If you moved back to Oklahoma, you would recognize the offices. If you used California’s system with Oklahoma habits—show up unannounced for a license and a title on the same afternoon—you would bounce off the appointment wall.

In 2010, the UN General Assembly voted 122–0 to recognize clean water and sanitation as a human right. The US abstained, saying access to water wasn’t a right under existing international law.

The Pro models come with up to 2TB storage. Apple has significantly upgraded battery life and cameras. Powered by the new A20 Pro chip, the iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback, while the Pro Max offers up to 45 hours.

The camera system gets a new 48MP Fusion main camera with variable aperture, which Apple calls one of its biggest camera upgrades in years.

Apple also unveiled the Apple Watch Series 12, Apple Watch Ultra 4 and AirPods 5, priced at $129.

text:
🚨UPDATE

To anyone claiming the U.S. 'started' this trade war with Canada: check the facts!

👉🏻Dairy: Canada protected its market with 300% tariffs on U.S. farmers for decades.
👉🏻Tech: Canada added Digital Taxes specifically targeting U.S. innovation.

👉🏻Reciprocity: Canada expected 100% free access to our economy while keeping theirs protected.

Prime Minister Mark Carney’s administration operated under the assumption that the U.S. would forever accept an asymmetric relationship. 

President Trump’s insistence on trade reciprocity is NOT an escalation; it is a necessary, long overdue rebalancing to ensure American workers, farmers & businesses are treated fairly. 

🚨 WHAT THE U.S. OFFERED - AND WHAT CARNEY DEMANDED AND AND WHAT ACTUALLY MOVED

👉🏻U.S. offers on the table:
▫️ Lower tariffs on Canadian steel & aluminum
▫️ Reduced tariffs on Canadian autos (toward 15% with U.S.-content carve-outs)
▫️ Elimination of a lumber tariff
▫️ Prospect of the best treatment of any major exporter to the U.S. market

👉🏻 In return the United States sought:
▫️ Removal of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum & autos.
▫️ Restoration of U.S. alcohol sales in provincial liquor systems
▫️ Real improvement in dairy market access - specifically fixing the restrictive tariff-rate quota (TRQ) allocation rules that have long limited U.S. cheese & other dairy products.
▫️ Removal of Canada’s retaliatory tariffs
▫️ Reciprocal treatment that did not further disadvantage American producers on auto content and truck categories.

👉🏻What Canada offered / conceded:
▫️ Willingness to drop its existing retaliatory tariffs on U.S. steel, aluminum & autos.
▫️ Willingness to “encourage” provinces to put U.S. alcohol back on shelves.

👉🏻What Canada demanded / pushed for:
▫️ Better tariff treatment specifically for medium & heavy duty trucks (not just light vehicles)
▫️ More favorable treatment of Canadian content in auto calculations
▫️ Broader relief that would keep Canadian auto, steel & aluminum production fully economic under the new rates
▫️ Resistance to changes on dairy TRQ administration & provincial alcohol restrictions

👉🏻 What did not meaningfully move:
On the single most important issue for American dairy farmers - the restrictive TRQ allocation system - Canada offered NO substantial structural change. 

Carney treated meaningful reform of dairy supply management rules as a threat to Canadian industries & sovereignty.

🚨Net result:
Canada was prepared to unwind some of its own retaliatory measures & partially address the alcohol bans but gave NO significant new market access relief on dairy - the barrier that has most directly hurt American farmers - while still demanding major tariff reductions from the United States. 

👀👉🏻That is why the U.S. side viewed the final Canadian position as insufficient reciprocity.

Carney publicly stated the U.S. “asked too much and offered too little” & that the terms threatened key Canadian industries and sovereignty. 

He suspended the talks & moved to dollar-for-dollar retaliation covering $20-27.6B in American goods.

That ignored the leverage reality. Canada depends on the American market. America does not depend on Canada to the same degree. Walking away from relief on Canada’s key export sectors & choosing escalation put the heavier costs on Canadian exporters & workers.

👀👉🏻 Next post: The real costs Canadian barriers have already imposed on Americans.

🚨 CARNEY PICKED A FIGHT WITH THE CUSTOMER THAT BUYS MOST OF CANADA’S EXPORTS -  AND NOW CANADIAN COMPANIES ARE BEING CUT OUT OF $50 BILLION IN U.S. GOVERNMENT CONTRACTS

@MarkJCarney decided to escalate a tariff war against the United States. 

                               That was a bad call.

Canada sends roughly 3/4s of its exports to America. The United States is not equally dependent on Canada. 

💥When you start a trade fight with the customer that buys most of what you sell, you should expect consequences.

This afternoon @POTUS Trump directed the General Services Administration, working with the @USTradeRep , to begin REMOVING Canadian origin products from the GSA Multiple Award Schedules - the federal government’s main purchasing catalog that moves more than $50B a year - unless Canada restores full & fair reciprocity for American farmers & companies.

👀👉🏻 Perhaps Carney thinks he can replace lost American demand by cutting a big new trade deal with China & its 1.4 billion people.

                           Good luck with that, Carney. 

Canada still does NOT have the pipelines, the large scale tanker terminals, or the refining flexibility to suddenly redirect massive volumes of oil & other exports across the Pacific. 

👉🏻It runs into hard logistical walls: limited pipeline capacity to the west coast, restricted tanker terminal space, the Oil Tanker Moratorium on parts of the northern British Columbia coast, longer shipping distances, higher costs & refiners on the other side of the ocean that are NOT set up to absorb Canadian heavy crude at the same scale the United States already does.

Those constraints are NOT TALKING POINTS - they are physical & logistical facts. 

The United States, meanwhile, keeps the customer relationship that already buys the large majority of what Canada sells & simply shifts its own federal purchasing to domestic or other eligible suppliers.

🚨Sorry, Canadians, your Prime Minister picked a fight with the market that actually sustains your export economy - & with a President who puts American citizens first.

             Carney is outmatched & every way that matters.

The heavier economic pain is landing on the Canadian side.

The United States, meanwhile, keeps its largest customer relationship & simply shifts federal buying to domestic or other eligible suppliers.

🚨 In a Nutshell
▫️ Trump ordered steps to remove Canadian-origin products from the GSA Multiple Award Schedules.
▫️ That catalog handles more than $50 billion in federal purchases every year.
▫️ The move is tied to Canadian barriers that limit American companies in Canada’s government procurement markets.
▫️ Canada depends on the U.S. market far more than the reverse.
▫️ Pivoting to China sounds nice on paper but runs into real infrastructure and logistics limits.
▫️ This is the predictable result of choosing escalation over a realistic deal.

👀👉🏻 Next post: What the GSA Schedule actually is and why losing it hurts Canadian firms.

Sources: President Trump’s September 8, 2026 directive; GSA Multiple Award Schedule program data.

text:
I built STIA, Sports Trading Intelligence Agent, an AI agent designed to analyze sports prediction markets, particularly football markets on @Polymarket, and help traders make one simple decision:

TRADE or PASS.

STIA scans Polymarket markets using data from the CLOB and Gamma APIs, combines that with football statistics through sports data APIs, additional scraping, and its own probability analysis to estimate fair probabilities and identify potential trading edges.

I’ve been building and refining this for months because I didn’t want another tool that simply gives you a prediction.

I wanted something that could actually study the market before you put your money into it.

Once I had the system in a state I was comfortable testing, I decided to put it through a real experiment.

During the World Cup, I started tracking the positions and analysis generated by STIA, recording both wins and losses. I also expanded the experiment across fixtures from the top European leagues since the football season began in August, as well as the current UEFA Champions League.

The idea is simple:

Don’t blindly trade a market just because you think you know the outcome. Understand the price first.

Polymarket can sometimes overprice or underprice football outcomes.

And that difference between the market price and what the available data suggests the probability should actually be, can create an opportunity, or tell you to stay away.

For example, take Barcelona vs Feyenoord in the Champions League.

STIA's estimated fair probability for the Barcelona outcome was around 87–89%, while the market was pricing it around 91.5¢.

At that price, the risk/reward wasn't attractive enough to justify taking the position.

Instead, STIA identified potentially more interesting opportunities in other markets, including BTTS around 53.5¢ and the Over 4.5 Goals market.

That’s exactly what I wanted STIA to do.

Not tell you to trade every market. Sometimes the best decision a trading agent can give you is:

PASS.

The goal is to use football probabilities, statistics, market pricing and probability analysis to understand whether the price you're being offered actually makes sense.

I basically decided to code my way out of blindly trading.

I’m still testing, refining and trying to make STIA better before releasing it publicly.

And yes, it will be free.

If you trade football prediction markets, especially on Polymarket, I’ll be sharing more about STIA and the results from its ongoing testing.

Because understanding the market before opening a position will always be better than trading without understanding what you're actually buying ⚽📊

text:
Hosea 9

1 Rejoice not, O Israel, for joy, as other people: for thou hast gone a whoring from thy God, thou hast loved a reward upon every cornfloor.

2 The floor and the winepress shall not feed them, and the new wine shall fail in her.

3 They shall not dwell in the LORD's land; but Ephraim shall return to Egypt, and they shall eat unclean things in Assyria.

4 They shall not offer wine offerings to the LORD, neither shall they be pleasing unto him: their sacrifices shall be unto them as the bread of mourners; all that eat thereof shall be polluted: for their bread for their soul shall not come into the house of the LORD.

5 What will ye do in the solemn day, and in the day of the feast of the LORD?

6 For, lo, they are gone because of destruction: Egypt shall gather them up, Memphis shall bury them: the pleasant places for their silver, nettles shall possess them: thorns shall be in their tabernacles.

7 The days of visitation are come, the days of recompence are come; Israel shall know it: the prophet is a fool, the spiritual man is mad, for the multitude of thine iniquity, and the great hatred.

8 The watchman of Ephraim was with my God: but the prophet is a snare of a fowler in all his ways, and hatred in the house of his God.

9 They have deeply corrupted themselves, as in the days of Gibeah: therefore he will remember their iniquity, he will visit their sins.

10 I found Israel like grapes in the wilderness; I saw your fathers as the firstripe in the fig tree at her first time: but they went to Baalpeor, and separated themselves unto that shame; and their abominations were according as they loved.

11 As for Ephraim, their glory shall fly away like a bird, from the birth, and from the womb, and from the conception.

12 Though they bring up their children, yet will I bereave them, that there shall not be a man left: yea, woe also to them when I depart from them!

13 Ephraim, as I saw Tyrus, is planted in a pleasant place: but Ephraim shall bring forth his children to the murderer.

14 Give them, O LORD: what wilt thou give? give them a miscarrying womb and dry breasts.

text:
The Nokia 3310 wasn't just a mobile phone; it was a masterpiece of biomechanical empathy. 

Long before the era of fragile, oversized glass slabs that demand our constant visual attention, this softly rounded device was designed entirely around the human hand. Its subtle curves and satisfying density nested perfectly into the palm, making it feel less like a piece of cold technology and more like a natural extension of your own body.
There was a singular, pure dignity in its purpose. 

It existed to connect you to another human voice, unburdened by the relentless noise of notifications, endless scrolling, or the anxiety of a rapidly draining battery. Because it was built to serve one core function, it did it flawlessly. Its compact, elegant silhouette slipped effortlessly into a pocket, completely unobtrusive until it demanded attention with that iconic, piercing monophonic ringtone.

The true magic of the device lived in its keypad. The layout was a triumph of tactile design, featuring perfectly spaced, distinct keys that offered an incredibly satisfying physical click. It was so intuitively mapped to the natural sweeping arc of a thumb that an entire generation learned to type out messages at lightning speed without ever needing to glance down at the monochrome green screen. It was a rhythmic, muscle-memory dance—a deeply tactile experience that modern flat touchscreens have entirely erased.

And then there was its legendary, near-mythical resilience. The 3310 didn't require an aftermarket protective case because it was the armor. A dropped phone didn't elicit a gasp of panic or a shattered screen; at worst, it meant picking up the battery, snapping the indestructible navy-blue plastic shell back into place, and powering it right back on. It was a device built with a profound respect for the real world, a world of concrete, gravity, and daily wear and tear. 

In its beautiful simplicity, unbreakable durability, and perfect harmony with human touch, the Nokia 3310 stands as one of the greatest, most unpretentious pieces of electronics ever built by man.

text:
The Ford 300 inline-six delivered freight for 31 years. The Iron Duke delivered mail for 30. The Ford 2.3 Lima delivered groceries in Pintos for 23 years and then won a European touring car championship. The same engine. The one from the Pinto. The one from the Mustang II. The base four-cylinder that nobody ordered by choice in any car it was ever installed in. It won nine of twelve rounds in the British Saloon Car Championship because a man named Andy Rouse turned up the boost and discovered that two valves per cylinder was enough when the turbocharger was doing the breathing.
Ford introduced the 2.3 Lima for 1974 as its first metric-displacement engine for North America. 140 cubic inches. Iron block. Iron head. Belt-driven single overhead cam working through finger followers. The most modern valvetrain Ford offered in an economy car and simultaneously the least exciting engine in Ford's entire lineup. It went into the Pinto, the Mustang II, the Fairmont, the Ranger, and the early Aerostar. Built at the Lima plant in Ohio with additional production at Taubate, Brazil. Twenty-three years of production from 1974 through 1997. The kind of engine that exists in a car buyer's memory as "I think it was a four-cylinder" and nothing more.
Then Ford added a turbocharger and the engine changed character completely. The 1979 Fox-body Mustang got a turbocharged 2.3 as an alternative to the V8. The 1983 Thunderbird Turbo Coupe added port fuel injection. The 1984 Mustang SVO added an intercooler, creating the most sophisticated four-cylinder Ford had ever offered in a production car: 175 HP climbing to 205 by 1986 from 140 cubic inches. More horsepower per cubic inch than the 302 V8 it shared the Mustang lineup with. The SVO was the car for the buyer who cared about technology more than displacement. There were not many of those buyers in 1984 America. The V8 Mustang GT outsold the SVO by margins that made accountants nervous.
The unexpected chapter happened three thousand miles away. By April 1985, Ford had homologated 5,000 Merkur XR4Ti models for Group A competition. The XR4Ti was a rebadged Ford Sierra with the turbocharged 2.3 Lima under the hood, built for the American market but carrying the homologation numbers that European racing required. Andy Rouse entered one in the British Saloon Car Championship, racing against Rover V8 powered cars that had more cylinders, more displacement, and more prestige. Rouse described the engine in terms that would make any marketing department cry: basic. Two valves per cylinder. Nothing exotic.
Then he turned up the boost. More power and more torque than the Rovers. Nine wins in twelve rounds. A fourth British championship title for Rouse. Won with a Pinto engine. The same iron block and iron head architecture that had been hauling mulch in Rangers and commuting in Fairmonts since Gerald Ford was president. The same finger followers. The same belt-driven single overhead cam. The same 140 cubic inches. With a turbocharger and a man who understood that displacement is an ingredient and boost is a multiplier. Rouse multiplied 140 cubic inches past everything the Rovers could answer with naturally aspirated V8s.
The 2.3 Lima is the proof that no engine is too humble for greatness if somebody adds boost and isn't concerned about its resume. The Pinto engine. The Ranger engine. The Mustang II engine. The engine that won a European touring car championship because Andy Rouse read the boost gauge instead of the badge on the valve cover. Nine of twelve rounds. Two valves per cylinder. From Lima, Ohio, to a British championship. The most unlikely title any Ford engine has ever won.

🏛️ The Jury Proof Gap: Why Your Story Needs a Framework
To an insurance company, a case that relies solely on a plaintiff describing their own pain is inherently more difficult to prove in front of a jury. Insurers don’t doubt your reality out of ignorance; they weaponize the lack of objective data to minimize your financial recovery.

To force a premium settlement, your personal testimony must align with a strategic medical foundation:

The Power of "Dovetailing": A high-value injury case requires a robust medical treatment team whose consistent clinical notes and records perfectly match, explain, and validate your daily struggles.

Objective Validation: When independent doctors, specialists, and therapists document your ongoing symptoms over time, your subjective pain gains objective legal weight.

Eliminating Insurance Leverage: A seamless medical history effectively bridges the gap between what you feel and what a jury can easily see, leaving the insurance company with no choice but to pay what your case is worth.

🎯 How to Maximize Your Case Value
If you are navigating an ongoing injury claim, your physical rehabilitation and your legal strategy are deeply connected. Don't let an adversarial insurance carrier minimize your daily struggles just because of a gap in documentation.

Speak with your legal team, ask the right questions, and find out exactly what steps you need to take to ensure your medical history fully supports the story you tell in court. ⚖️
