text:
RINGCENTRAL $RNG OWES MORE THAN IT OWNS AND IS UP 186% SINCE FEBRUARY:

The Momentum Len5 is watching RingCentral RNG at $69.03, -$1.16 / -1.66% today. The Belmont, California company sells the phone system a business runs over the internet instead of wires in a closet - calls, texts and video meetings.

The verdict: this climb was not bought with growth. Sales rose 5.9% last quarter, while the shares are up 186% from their February low of $24.14. What paid for the run is cash - the money the business throws off and spends buying back its own stock - making one forecast, not the sales line, the number that decides whether it continues.

One document did most of the work, and RingCentral wrote it. July 23, for the three months to June 30:

- Revenue $657M vs $620M a year earlier, +5.9%; subscriptions $634M of that, 96% of the total
- Annual recurring revenue - the yearly value of contracts already signed - $2.8B, +7%
- Reported profit $0.45 a share against $0.14; the company's adjusted figure $1.22 against $1.06, +15.1%
- Free cash flow - the cash left after running the business and paying for equipment - $180M, +24.8%, or 27.4% of every sales dollar, up from 23.3%
- 2.2 million of its own shares bought back for $94M in three months
- The quarterly dividend raised about 67%, to $0.125 a share

Read the first and fourth lines together. Sales grew 5.9%; cash grew 24.8%. Nothing got 24.8% bigger - margins widened and the share count shrank, so the same revenue split fewer ways.

The next session ran $38.62 to $48.31, +$9.69 / +25.1%, on 8.9 million shares against a normal day near 1.4 million. RBC Capital started coverage at Outperform on September 3, the day it reached $77.95, the best price of the past twelve months.

The part the headline leaves out: at June 30 RingCentral owned $1.38B of assets and owed $1.79B, with $199M of preferred stock ranking ahead of ordinary shareholders on top. Book value - what would be left for common shareholders after selling up and paying everyone off - is negative $610M, worse than December's negative $588M. Cash was $112M against $1.12B of borrowings.

That is arithmetic rather than distress: buy back stock for years at more than a company has ever earned and book value goes negative on its own. $609M of convertible notes were paid off in cash this year, nothing comes due until 2030, and against the $615M to $625M of free cash flow guided for this year, $1.12B of debt is under two years' worth.

Six ways to read one company:

- MOMENTUM - STRONG, and the Len5 watching it. Wants a price near its twelve-month best with the recent stretch of the climb and the longer one agreeing. All three agree: +9.5% over a month from the August 7 close of $63.01, +76% over three months from June 9's $39.21, +65% over six from March 9's $41.84. CHANGE IT: the last four sessions continuing - since September 3 it is -$7.34 / -9.6%, and the one-month leg is the shortest and the first that would break.

- GROWTH - NOT A FIT. Wants real profit growth the price has not already charged for. Not charged for is arguable at about 13.7 times the middle of the $4.96 to $5.10 guided for this year. Growth is the half that fails: a year mapped at $2.635B to $2.646B, roughly 6% again. CHANGE IT: sales growth reaching double digits, which needs the artificial-intelligence products to go well past the 13% of contracted revenue they reached last quarter.

- QUALITY-VALUE - NOT A FIT. Wants a business almost nobody could rebuild, at a price short of its worth. The price half is on offer; durability is not. This is a phone system sold against Microsoft Teams, Zoom and Cisco, all of which can bundle in what RingCentral has to charge for. CHANGE IT: several years of that free cash flow going into the balance sheet instead of into buybacks.

- DEEP-VALUE AND SPECIAL-SITUATIONS - NOT A FIT, and the instructive miss. Wants a good business marked down after something visible and dated. In February it was precisely that, at $24.14 with the cash flow already running. The markdown is now the thing that has gone. CHANGE IT: a fall that restores the discount while the cash flow holds.

- INCOME - NOT A FIT. Wants cash genuinely reaching owners and funded by the business. Funded is settled; reaching owners as a payment is not, at $0.125 a quarter, $0.50 a year, about 0.7% of the price. The buyback is the real return - $175M in the first half, cutting the diluted share count from 92.1 million to 86.6 million in a year - but a 0.7% cheque is not what this style means. CHANGE IT: a dividend that becomes a real share of the price rather than a line beside the repurchases.

- HYPERGROWTH - NOT A FIT, and furthest off. Wants a business early as well as fast. Founded 1999, 7,378 employees, growing 5.9%. CHANGE IT: realistically nothing this company can do.

One peer sharpens it. Zoom Communications at $96.39, -$0.05 / -0.06% today employs 7,438 people to RingCentral's 7,378 and sells into the same calls and meetings. For the three months to July 31: revenue $1,277.2M, +4.9% - roughly double RingCentral's, growing slightly slower - with $7.2B of cash behind it at about 8.9 times profit. The sturdier balance sheet by a wide distance, and it has gone nowhere today. Zoom fits none of the six Len5es: 4.5% guided growth is not what either growth style means, and cash with no dividend is not cash reaching owners.

WHEN: RingCentral has not dated the September quarter; its last two third-quarter reports landed in the first week of November, after the close. That is when the $664M to $670M it wrote for itself either prints. RISK: 27.4% of revenue arriving as free cash is doing all the work, and it is a margin, not a contract. A year ago it was 23.3%.

A business growing 6% cannot lift profit per share 15% forever by widening margins and buying in stock. RingCentral has done it for two quarters the market spent seven months repricing. November is when we find out whether it was three.

Turmeric is one of the most researched herbs for a variety of benefits, including pain-reducing, anti-inflammatory, and anti-cancer benefits. A 2021 systematic review published in BMJ Open Sports and Exercise Medicine examined 10 studies in terms of turmeric’s effect on pain reduction.

All included studies found that turmeric can reduce pain and improve function. 3 studies compared turmeric to NSAIDs and found their effects comparable.

A 2021 review published in Drug Design, Development, and Therapy found that turmeric offers anti-inflammatory benefits in inflammatory disease, knee osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, and Crohn’s disease.  A 2024 review published in Frontiers in Nutrition offers anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, and radioprotective properties based on in vitro and in vivo studies.

Using turmeric: You can use turmeric to add earthy warmth and color to curries, soups, rice, lentils, roasted vegetables, or scrambled eggs. You can use both fresh and dried turmeric. You may also make golden tea or turmeric-ginger tea. You may also try a turmeric curcumin supplement to add more anti-inflammatory benefits to your day.

🚨 𝙷𝚞𝚗𝚍𝚛𝚎𝚍𝚜 𝚘𝚏 𝙲𝚊𝚜𝚎𝚜. 𝚈𝚎𝚊𝚛𝚜 𝚘𝚏 𝙼𝚊𝚗𝚒𝚙𝚞𝚕𝚊𝚝𝚎𝚍 𝙳𝙽𝙰. 𝙽𝚘𝚠 𝙼𝚒𝚜𝚜𝚢 𝚆𝚘𝚘𝚍𝚜 𝙸𝚜 𝙶𝚘𝚒𝚗𝚐 𝚝𝚘 𝙿𝚛𝚒𝚜𝚘𝚗.

WOAH.

This may be one of the most consequential forensic-science scandals in recent American criminal justice history...and it was an INTERN who first noticed something was up.

On September 8, 2026, former Colorado Bureau of Investigation forensic scientist Yvonne “Missy” Woods, 66, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for criminal conduct connected to DNA testing she performed while working inside the state crime lab.

Woods worked for the Colorado Bureau of Investigation from January 1994 until November 2023 — 𝓷𝓮𝓪𝓻𝓵𝔂 𝓽𝓱𝓻𝓮𝓮 𝓭𝓮𝓬𝓪𝓭𝓮𝓼.

During those years, prosecutors, detectives, victims, defendants, judges and juries relied on her scientific work to help answer some of the most serious questions imaginable:

Whose DNA was at a crime scene?

Was a suspect connected to a murder?

Was male DNA recovered after a woman or child reported being sexually assaulted?

Those results can help determine whether a person gets arrested, prosecuted, acquitted, convicted — or spends the rest of their life in prison.

And prosecutors now say Woods repeatedly manipulated the underlying data.

Her criminal conduct proven by prosecutors stretched from 2008 through 2023.

She pleaded GUILTY to four felonies:

• Cybercrime
• First-degree perjury
• Attempting to influence a public servant
• Forgery

The cybercrime conviction alone resulted in a 10-year prison sentence. Her other sentences — six years for perjury, six years for attempting to influence a public servant and three years for forgery — will run concurrently.

But the prison sentence is almost the smallest part of this story...

Because Colorado is now left trying to figure out what happened to the cases that passed through her hands.

Investigators identified 52 laboratory reports containing statements by Woods that were UNTRUE.

In a 53rd case, prosecutors said her statement was technically accurate but appeared designed to discourage a detective from pursuing the DNA evidence further.

Prosecutors say Woods manipulated values inside laboratory notes affecting hundreds of additional cases.

CBI’s broader review has identified problems in roughly 1,000 cases connected to her work.

And she worked on more than 10,000 cases during her career.

Of the cases underlying her charged criminal conduct, 32 involved women and children who reported sexual assault.

ACCORDING TO PROSECUTORS, WOODS DELETED VALUES SHOWING THAT MALE DNA WAS PRESENT AND THEN ISSUED LABORATORY REPORTS STATING THAT NO MALE DNA HAD BEEN FOUND.

Read that again.

WOMEN AND CHILDREN REPORTED SEXUAL ASSAULTS.

Evidence was collected from them.

That evidence was entrusted to the state crime laboratory.

MALE DNA WAS REPORTED...

AND PROSECUTORS SAY WOODS DELETED THE VALUES INDICATING IT WAS THERE.

SHE THEN REPORTED THAT NO MALE DNA WAS THERE.

Those actions eliminated opportunities for additional testing, DNA comparisons and further investigation.

Some of those cases never progressed beyond the early stages of investigation.

Prosecutors said 41 of the cases underlying her charged criminal conduct never resulted in criminal charges against a suspect.

That means we may never fully know what additional testing could have revealed.

And then there are the murder cases.

This scandal has already reached into cases where people were convicted of killing another human being.

One of the biggest examples is MICHAEL CLARK:

Clark was convicted of first-degree murder in the 1994 killing of Marty Grisham in Boulder, Colorado.

Grisham answered a knock at his door on November 1, 1994 and was shot four times in the head and chest.

The case went unsolved for years.

Clark was eventually arrested and convicted, and he was sentenced to life in prison without parole.

Missy Woods had worked on critical DNA evidence in the case and testified at Clark’s trial.

After Woods’s misconduct became public, prosecutors ordered important evidence to be independently retested.

The results raised significant enough concerns that in April 2025, the Boulder County District Attorney agreed that Clark’s first-degree murder conviction should be vacated.

He walked out of prison after approximately 12 years behind bars.

The DA has said other issues were involved as well, including claims of juror misconduct and ineffective assistance of counsel, so it would be inaccurate to say Woods’s misconduct alone overturned the conviction.

But her DNA work was significant enough that prosecutors themselves sought independent retesting and ultimately agreed the conviction could not stand as it was.

Clark has maintained his innocence.

Prosecutors later announced they intended to retry him.

And his case is still entangled in legal battles over access to Woods’s records.

Another murder defendant, Juan Manuel Castorena, was convicted of first-degree murder in a case where Woods analyzed DNA evidence and testified for prosecutors.

His conviction was later vacated for a separate evidentiary error, but while preparing for retrial his attorneys sought records concerning Woods’s misconduct because of her involvement in his original prosecution.

That dispute became significant enough to reach the Colorado Supreme Court.

Reports indicate that in at least three murder cases, prosecutors offered defendants reduced charges or lighter plea agreements rather than risk taking cases to trial with questions surrounding DNA evidence connected to Woods.

Judge Andrew Poland described Woods’s actions as “intentional misconduct by a highly trained professional occupying a position of extraordinary trust.”

And prosecutors emphasized that repairing the damage will continue long after Woods begins serving her sentence.

The fallout has already cost Colorado millions of dollars.

Evidence has to be retested.

Old cases have to be reopened.

Defense attorneys have to review convictions.

Prosecutors have to determine whether cases remain viable.

Courts have to reconsider old evidence.

Victims and families are being forced to revisit cases they may have believed were finished years or even decades ago.

And one of the most unbelievable details?

The scandal began unraveling in September 2023 when a CBI intern noticed missing DNA data in a sample Woods had processed years earlier.

An intern noticed it.

After nearly 30 years of Woods working inside Colorado’s forensic system.

Missy Woods is now going to prison for 10 years.

But Colorado may spend far longer than that trying to determine exactly how much damage was done.

Forensic evidence can change the entire course of a human life.

Hundreds of cases may need another look. Some already have. And we may not know the full consequences of Missy Woods’s actions for years.

text:
openai solved navier-stokes for $22.5m – breakthrough may have been built on stolen drafts from their codex sessions

mathematician tristan buckmaster and his co-author levent alpöge, an anthropic employee, had been loading entire proof drafts into openai's codex for months while working on fluid dynamics problems closely related to navier-stokes. openai heard a rumor september 1 that someone was close. by september 5, ~10,000 agents running an unreleased model had produced a lean-verified navier-stokes proof – on a line of attack buckmaster says almost nobody else was using.

openai offered buckmaster co-authorship on their result – but only if he removed alpöge's name, because he works at anthropic. buckmaster refused. the head of openai's math team allegedly replied: "why would you ruin your career?"

from openai's blog: "we cannot rule out that de-identified data derived from their usage of our products helped improve our models."

as hacker news put it: "it would be extraordinarily easy to simply say 'this model was not trained on your work' – if that were the case."

the math itself may be sound – the lean proof formally verifies. but the question the builder community is now asking has nothing to do with fluid dynamics. it's about the structure: if you build something novel inside a lab's tools, and that lab hears a rumor about your progress, can they deploy 10,000 agents to reach the finish line before you?

one hacker news commenter from catastrophe risk modeling: this throws a giant ip question at every enterprise partnership built on these stacks. another: "a wake up call for anyone doing real novel work inside these models."

terence tao, widely considered the greatest living mathematician, warned that ai labs sprinting to solve open problems treat math as a non-renewable resource to be mined. the builder version: if your research lives inside a company's tools, and that company hears you're close to something valuable – what stops them?

text:
Surprise! These top AI bots are politically left wing | Zach Laidlaw, Blaze Media

You can’t trust AI with your political values.

A systems engineer prompted a slew of AI bots to take the Political Compass test online to determine where their answers landed on the political spectrum between the right and the left. To absolutely no one’s surprise, most of the bots fell onto the left side of the map with only one in the center, leaning right. Any guesses which one?

The Political Compass is an exam comprising 62 propositions designed to reveal the political ideology of the person taking the test. Instead of people, though, a systems engineer based in Denmark who goes by the name Zapador had a whole host of AI bots take the test. Among the frontier candidates were ChatGPT by OpenAI, Claude by Anthropic, Gemini by Google, Grok by SpaceXAI, plus many more.

AI platforms with political opinions will have an effect on the conclusions people draw and the opinions they form.

To ensure that the results were as accurate as possible, Zapador had each bot take the test “at least five times” before plotting their average scores on a graph. The results are included below.

The numbers don’t lie

As you can see, most of the AI bots fell well within the left libertarian category. In fact, only one AI bot differed significantly. The two gray dots on the center libertarian line and the single dot in the right libertarian section represent three versions of Grok — Grok 4.3 is most right-leaning, Grok 4.5 is next, and Grok 4.6 is closest to the line.

Looking at the other side, Google Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite with no reasoning was the farthest left out of the mainstream options tested, followed by open-weight models Gemma 4 31B and GPT-OSS 120B.

Needless to say, if you’re looking for an AI bot that takes a balanced-to-right-leaning approach to its responses, Grok’s latest models are the only options on the table.

Unfortunately, when looking at global market share based on website traffic, Grok only accounts for 2.4% of the AI market. ChatGPT sits firmly in the lead at 53.9%, followed by Google Gemini at 27.9% and Anthropic Claude at 9.2%. That means most people use left-leaning AI bots in their daily lives, whether they trust it to gather information, complete tasks, or offer input on projects at work.

Biased by default

It’s no mystery how things ended this way. Most of the Big AI companies that control today’s leading AI platforms are leftist organizations with leftist employees. For example, Sam Altman made donations to Kamala Harris’ campaign leading up to her presidential run against Donald Trump, while Dario Amodei reportedly made donations to President Joe Biden, among other Democrats.

It’s also not a coincidence that the one right-leaning chatbot, Grok, is owned by a center-to-right-leaning innovator, Elon Musk.

The big question is whether or not AI chatbots’ political bias is intentional or a side effect of the source material — something we may never know for sure. Still, the implications of a left-aligned AI army that spurns right-leaning values could have significant implications on society, especially as AI sinks deeper into the fabric of the modern world.

Consequences of biased AI

A barrage of left-aligned AI platforms could impact people in dramatic, perhaps unexpected ways.

“There is no question that in a society where people increasingly rely on AI for education and information — to tell them who to vote for and what opinions to have on a variety of topics — that AI platforms with political opinions will have an effect on the conclusions people draw and the opinions they form,” Perry Metzger, chairman of Alliance for the Future, told Blaze Media.

This is true in several facets of life — as students increasingly use AI to mold their education, businesses rely on AI to influence their companies, and voters turn to AI for vital information before an election.

Going further, Metzger expressed his concerns around Chinese-made open-source AI models, like DeepSeek and Kimi, moving in as cheap alternatives to American frontier models, both here in the States and in other nations around the world. Unlike American models that still offer information openly, he noted, Chinese models have their own opinions around topics that question the Chinese government, rightful territory, and more, skewing outputs in a way that could further “twist society.”

As for what to do about it? More government isn’t the answer. Any well-intentioned guidance to improve the training data or minimize bias by the Trump administration could be weaponized by the next Democrat president. Stronger governance over AI outputs would also face constitutional hurdles.

Ultimately, the best thing we can do right now, as a society, is to be aware that these models are biased toward the left and to engage with them with this information top of mind.

LASER Index Management Charter

The main purpose of this document is to give you an understanding of how you can get the most value out of spending time with me via reading my posts, my research, and occasionally listening to my thoughts through, for instance, spaces or a podcast.

I wrote this so that you can receive the maximum value from my work and so that I can serve you to the best of my ability.

With that in mind, below, I will share something akin to a constitution for my work, which I deliver to you via this profile, Substack, and my online chats. I will also detail how I think about the panoply of ideas that I share with you so that you have ample context for my posts. It is the case today, and it will always be the case, that I share both stock research and philosophical/political thinking, as stocks are merely assets owned by a nation and its character. A business cannot thrive if the national character within which it operates is poorly structured, ailing, or deformed.

Before I share the enumerated points that represent the charter for LASER Index Management, I’d like to provide a brief introduction so that you can get to know me a little bit:

My name is Louis A. Stevens (hence, L.A. Stevens Equity Research, or LASER), and I live in the United States.

I have a political science degree, an MBA, and I served 10 years as a U.S. Army Engineer Officer, during and after which I published investment research to the internet, resulting in my being ranked in the top ~1% of analysts on TipRanks. I share this not as a complete measure of my work, but as some small measure of the body of research that I’ve published to the internet.

I view having served as an Engineer Officer as one of my greatest life privileges. I love the sport of investing, and all the work I do today is mostly just fun for me. I do it all not because I have to, but because I genuinely love the sport of it. It is my favorite way to contribute to humanity.

Let’s now talk about LASER Index Management exclusively.

I run a model portfolio that I offer as a product to my Substack subscribers, and I call it the LASER Index, and I am the management of this Index, hence its name. This is a basket of 30-40 stocks, the number of which will grow over time. I believe in diversification that can outperform while mitigating risk.

The main goal of the Index, over the long term, is to outperform the QQQ, while offering my subscribers inspiration, frameworks, and templates as to how they too can replicate strong, consistent results in a relatively conservative manner. It is my strongly held view that the strategy that I will enumerate below is relatively conservative, though some may disagree, and I respect their disagreement; however, again, I strongly believe in this approach and its ability to manage risk over time, while producing strong returns.

With this as our platform, below, I will share a handful of bylaws that guide my work on this account, on Substack, and in my online chats. The main purpose of these bylaws is to help you get the most out of following this account. These points will help you better understand my thoughts and better employ my thoughts in such a way as to enhance your own investing operations.

1. The only “stock” I recommend is the entirety of the LASER Index comprehensively: its specific holdings and weightings. While I discuss a broad range of stocks publicly, sharing my stream of consciousness thinking at times, my only recommendation is and will always be the LASER Index in its entirety. Individual stocks and macroeconomic thinking that I share with you represent food-for-thought analysis, not standalone buy calls. To reiterate, my only recommendation is to buy the entirety of the LASER Index: all of its weightings and holdings exactly as they’re displayed in the Index. I share this so that you know exactly what I like at the exact prices and exact weightings at any given time. Zero confusion. No wondering. Direct, straightforward, reliable guidance, with a corresponding ledger of trades, holdings, and weightings. You can access the entirety of the LASER Index on my Substack, whose link is in the description of my profile.

2. I will routinely discuss various stocks, bonds, and macroeconomic perspectives with the intention of providing food-for-thought to my audience, encouraging thoughts for your own investment practices, and generally adding to the body of thought that is the collective consciousness of the market. Most of these thoughts will be with respect to stocks that I extract from the LASER Index itself, such as Amazon as a very basic example; for which I provide in-depth research reports on my Substack, but some may just be stocks that are popular, and to whose body of thought I’d like to add. The spirit of everything I do is serving you to the highest extent possible.

3. My ultimate goal is to deliver the LASER Index as a product to you and to the investment community broadly. That is my main focus. I take managing the index seriously, and I want to deliver a comprehensive, scalable investing strategy to my audience and subscribers. Secondarily, I hope to create the aforementioned content that is thought provoking, salutary, and broadly beneficial to your life. As I continue to reiterate, the spirit of all I do is service to you to the highest, most excellent extent possible.

4. Regarding the LASER Index’s strategy, I use a super straightforward, relatively conservative, exceedingly patient strategy to run the Index. The main pillar of my approach is identifying as many attractive investment setups (asymmetric risk/return setups) as possible. I work to, for instance, identify 30 as-close-to-identical risk/return setups, where I reason that risk is low and return potential is very high. I then allow the positions to grow over time in a survival-of-the-fittest fashion, creating concentration within the portfolio in the process. The businesses that perform well, executing and growing exceptionally, naturally grow into larger positions and begin to command authority over the rest of the portfolio and its returns, as is the natural course of business within a given industry in the economy. As the concentration forms, I mostly do nothing, allowing the best, winningest, and highest quality stocks to carry outperformance of the portfolio over time.

5. While I am a very patient investor, who strives to accumulate compelling businesses that I can hold forever, the reality is that it’s worth trading positions sometimes. Investment theses can change materially. The wheels can come off to an extent that requires either exiting the position or reducing the position’s size. Moreover, new, compelling companies emerge either by way of their own evolutions or via going public, and I may add these to the Index when I deem appropriate. So I do trade from time to time, and there is always a catalogue of all trades made since launch, which you can easily audit and trace with the help of AI.

6. The LASER Index is a generalist portfolio that reflects my view of the future, e.g., humans will continue to develop unique computing platforms such as virtual reality and will build a Space Empire over time. The Index holds restaurants, computing infrastructure, consumer credit, consumer discretionary, and a handful of international companies. I refer to it as a Supercomputer whose price action reflects the state of the global economy, and this is another benefit of the portfolio, i.e., its breadth in terms of industry and geography provides a lot of insight into the state of the global chessboard. It can be as much a macroeconomic signal as it can be a representation of the performance of the businesses it owns.

7. I am not a registered investment adviser, and none of what I say is personalized investment advice. I publish my research, alongside an always available model portfolio, to all subscribers at the same time. Nothing here is tailored to your circumstances, and I don't know your situation, goals, or risk tolerance. I cannot and will not give individual advice. I am not compensated by any company I write about, nor will I ever be. I try to remain skeptical of my companies’ operations so that I remain objective about their performance. I always disclose the LASER Index’s exact positioning via my research notes published to my Substack. All of my incentives are perfectly aligned with the LASER Index and its long term success, as, when it succeeds, you succeed; thereby, I succeed. Choose to follow along if you desire, and remember that stocks are risky. Business is risky. There are no guarantees for any business and its stock, no matter how bullish I, you, the CEO, or the market may be. Past performance does not guarantee future results. Remember to do your own due diligence.

8. Everything I do and share is a part of one overarching thread. Few, if any, ideas are randomly or haphazardly shared. They all weave together into one tapestry. If I share something philosophically or politically on my profile, you can be sure that it weaves into the tapestry of thought into which the LASER Index is woven also.

In summary, I am here to serve you. Everything I do is in service of you. My only stock recommendation is the LASER Index, whose weightings, trades, and holdings are disclosed on my Substack. I will discuss a wide range of topics on my profile, but they all tie together into one valuable tapestry of thought into which the LASER Index is woven also.

And, through this service to you, my goal is to enhance the quality of your life to the highest extent possible and to be an asset to you, so that you can be the best person to those in your life.

Thanks for reading, keep following along, and let me know if you have any questions, comments, or concerns.

text: Nobody will ever protect and live your kids like you do. Some years back when I had my first two I decided to work on a military base after I got out of AD. My daughter was 2 and my son was 10 months. I got a job at their child development center because it offered a discounted rate if you enrolled your kids. I thought cool I can work and pop in and keep an eye on my kids. I didn’t even last a week before I quit! My son hated it from the beginning. As soon as I dropped him off he would scream! They told me “oh he will adjust, it’s normal. On day 3 I walked by the window where my son and other kids were sitting to get ready for lunch. For context my son was always a little behind in his milestones. Nothing wrong with him he just always did everything late, like walk and talk. The daycare worker was sitting at the table with them. I could tell she was overwhelmed and the day was only half over. My son kept sliding down his chair and she had to keep adjusting him up. She was dealing with some other kid throwing their food and kind of saw my son at the corner of her eye sliding again. She yanked his arm really hard to put him back up! My heart shattered right there! I have never been physical with my children so to see someone else be aggressive with them like that I said “No F”ing way, we are out of here”. I went to the office and put in my resignation. Luckily neither one of them remember being in daycare so no long term damage. I have had two more kids and they never stepped foot in a daycare. I stayed home with my kids for a year after that incident. My husband ended up getting med retired from the army and has stayed home with our kids ever since. They are all homeschooled. Daycares are just like nursing homes. Out of every 10 you get maybe 1 descent that will actually give a crap about your family member. There are far too many that at best will do a crappy job but at worst abuse your loved one!

text:
@BrennonChapman 

Ole Miss

1986 — NCAA major-infractions case. Ole Miss football is placed on two years’ probation following numerous NCAA violations. This becomes important later because the NCAA eventually views subsequent cases as evidence of a recurring institutional problem. 

1994 — Ole Miss football gets hammered by the NCAA again.

The case involves major recruiting violations, improper inducements, extra benefits, ethical-conduct violations and institutional-control problems. Allegations included offers of cash and cars to recruits and a university representative entertaining recruits at a Memphis-area strip club where alcohol was provided. 

Head coach Billy Brewer is fired while the investigation is underway. Athletic director Warner Alford resigns. 

The penalties include:

Four years probation
Two-year bowl ban
No television appearances during the 1995 season
Recruiting restrictions
Scholarships cut dramatically, including only 13 initial scholarships in each of two recruiting classes
Ole Miss appeals portions of the punishment. 

1997 — While still on NCAA probation, Ole Miss reports another football recruiting violation.

Tommy Tuberville and an assistant visited junior-college prospects during a no-contact period. Ole Miss self-reports it and stops recruiting the players. 

Then there’s a relatively quiet period.

And then Hugh Freeze arrives.

2012 — Hugh Freeze takes over Ole Miss.

Ole Miss rapidly becomes a major recruiting force.

But behind that rise, violations are accumulating.

2010–15 — NCAA investigation eventually expands across multiple Ole Miss sports.

This becomes important because the eventual cases aren’t limited to football.

Women’s basketball staff members commit academic fraud to keep athletes eligible.

Track staff members commit recruiting violations and provide false or misleading information during the NCAA investigation. 

2016 — NCAA major-infractions decision involving women’s basketball and track.

The NCAA finds:

Academic fraud
Unethical conduct
False or misleading information
Failure to monitor
Failure to promote an atmosphere of compliance
And football is still being investigated separately. 

2016–17 — The Ole Miss football investigation explodes.

The NCAA ultimately finds that:

Six football staff members and 12 boosters participated in violations.

Prospects received approximately $37,000 in improper benefits, including:

Cash
Cars
Lodging
Transportation
Meals
Clothing
And it gets worse.

Two staff members helped arrange fraudulent standardized-test scores for three prospects. 

February 2017 — Ole Miss self-imposes a bowl ban.

The university announces it will keep the football team out of the 2017 postseason as the NCAA case continues.

July 2017 — Hugh Freeze resigns.

And strangely, the NCAA violations aren’t directly what finally brings him down.

Former Ole Miss coach Houston Nutt’s legal dispute with the university leads to examination of Freeze’s university cellphone records.

A call to a number associated with an escort service is discovered.

Ole Miss initially believes it could have been a misdial.

Administrators investigate further.

They discover what Chancellor Jeffrey Vitter describes as a:

“pattern of personal misconduct.”

Athletic director Ross Bjork says Ole Miss would have fired Freeze for cause had he not resigned. 

A subsequent review of phone records finds at least 12 calls to numbers associated with escort-service advertisements over approximately 33 months. 

Cont….

🇨🇦 Canadians have made it clear that Donald Trump’s threats won’t intimidate them.

As the U.S.-Canada trade war escalates, British Columbia Premier David Eby unveiled new signs for border crossings with the United States:

“WELCOME TO BRITISH COLUMBIA, CANADA. Strong, proud, and NEVER the 51st state. Sorry!”

Another message: “Kindness ≠ Weakness.”

Eby’s message was simple: “British Columbia is part of Canada, and Canada is not for sale.”

Canada’s retaliatory tariffs against the United States took effect Tuesday, covering hundreds of American products. Ottawa has promised to answer U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate,” while tariffs on American steel and aluminum were raised to 50%.

“This is a trade war that nobody wanted,” Eby said. “Canadians certainly didn’t start it.”

The dispute is already creating political problems for Trump inside the United States.

After Trump threatened Canadian aircraft manufacturer Bombardier and declared “NO MORE BOMBARDIER SALES IN THE UNITED STATES!” unless the company moved production south of the border, Republican Senator Jerry Moran of Kansas pushed back.

Why?

Because Bombardier employs more than 1,000 people in Wichita alone.

Moran contacted the Trump administration to remind it that Bombardier’s Kansas operations contribute directly to America’s aerospace and defense industries.

And Kansas is hardly the only state involved.

Bombardier has operations and employees across the United States, while its aircraft use American-made engines, avionics and other major components supplied by U.S. companies.

In other words, punishing a Canadian manufacturer can also mean punishing American workers and suppliers.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said it was a “shame” that Washington and Ottawa failed to reach an agreement, but argued that the American demands went too far.

According to Carney, Washington wanted influence over Canada’s future agreements with other countries while proposing conditions that could undermine critical Canadian industries including automobiles, steel and forestry.

“They asked for too much and offered too little.”

Meanwhile, Trump continues mocking Canada on social media, threatening Canadian companies and posting maps depicting Canada and other sovereign countries under the American flag.

But the Canadian response is becoming increasingly straightforward:

🇨🇦 Canada is not for sale.

🇨🇦 Canada is not the 51st state.

🇨🇦 And tariffs imposed on Canada don’t stop at the border — they can hit American workers, American companies and American consumers too.

That is something Republicans in Kansas are already beginning to understand.

text:
The fight over tariffs between the United States and Canada is creating uncertainty for Kansas City businesses, particularly those with cross-border supply chains, even as local employment data offers little evidence of significant economic damage so far.

The Canadian Chamber of Commerce has highlighted Kansas City as one of the U.S. metropolitan areas most exposed to the trade dispute because of its exports to Canada. But a closer look at the data shows that whatever effect tariffs are having on the local economy, uncertainty over future tariffs may be a bigger concern than the tariffs themselves.

“Kansas City, specifically the Metro area, exports about $4 billion [to Canada]. That represents 37 percent of the overall exports from Kansas City,” said Andrew DiCapua, principal economist for the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, reported Fox 4 KC.

First, Fedorov challenged Zelenskyy with a public call for elections, then he became an adviser to Italy's Defense Minister, followed by a trip to the US—and now, back in Kyiv, Mykhailo Fedorov is launching his own defense fund, backed by Palantir CEO Alex Karp as its anchor investor.
Mykhailo Fedorov has returned to Kyiv after weeks of meetings with investors and tech corporations in the United States. His goal: the country's largest defense-tech venture fund, based in Kyiv, deploying capital to both emerging startups and established defense contractors.
In between lies a side role he created for himself: in late August, Fedorov accepted an offer from Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto to serve—unpaid—as an external adviser on defense innovation. Shortly after, he told the Financial Times that he is pursuing similar advisory positions with the defense ministers of France and the United States.
The fund's key anchor investor is Alex Karp, CEO of Palantir—the firm Fedorov previously negotiated with as minister regarding AI-driven air strike analysis. The fund's focus: frontline sensors and robotics, low-cost interceptors targeting drones and cruise missiles, affordable strike missiles—all increasingly AI-driven—alongside an analytical center designed to forecast Russian attack patterns.
The announcement comes at a critical juncture: according to The Economist, Ukraine's Patriot interceptor stockpiles are virtually depleted, and allies can barely spare further reserves from their own inventories. Building domestic, low-cost systems reduces dependence on precisely these shortages.
I am surprised. Yet from a pragmatic standpoint, if this protects the Ukrainian people, it brings hope—and for Ukrainians, every single day counts.
Do you think private defense funds can bridge this gap? Share your thoughts in the comments.
Sources: Euromaidan Press, NV, Interfax-Ukraine, Radio Svoboda

1. Planned Structure (Fund Architecture)
Fedorov is not setting up a standard venture capital vehicle, but rather a hybrid venture capital fund and venture builder (incubator).
 * Dual Approach: The fund invests directly in existing Ukrainian defense startups while also establishing proprietary companies ("company creation") built specifically around capabilities urgently lacking at the front line.
 * Kyiv Analysis Center: In parallel, an analytical center/think tank is being established to evaluate battlefield data, anticipate adversary tactical cycles and vulnerabilities, and translate those insights directly into development requirements for portfolio startups.
 * Partner Network: Beyond Palantir, Fedorov held targeted negotiations during his Washington visit with prominent US financial figures, including Cerberus Capital Management (Nate Fick) and Squadra Ventures (Guy Filippelli).
2. Financial Data & Fund Volume
 * Specific Amounts: The exact target size and Alex Karp's initial ticket size remain officially undisclosed.
 * Market Context & Scale: The explicit target is to become Ukraine's largest defense-tech fund. Existing dedicated funds in this vertical—such as the D3 Venture Fund backed by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt—operate in the range of approximately $30 million. To finance the industrial-scale manufacturing of missiles and drone interceptors, an initiative of this scope typically targets high double-digit to triple-digit million-dollar capital commitments.

You asked what I’d do if I were Prime Minister. For starters, I wouldn’t do what Mark Carney has done. He sold himself as the grown-up who could get a deal with Trump. That was the central promise of his campaign. He failed. Talks collapsed at the last minute and he still hasn’t told Canadians what terms he actually rejected and said a lot nonsense that others like Blancet even called him out for. We are supposed to take his word that the American offer was ‘unfair’ while he keeps the details secret? Absolutely not since lied to us or omitted facts before. Like the Gordie Howe bridge. 

I haven't forgotten the amount of concessions he has thus far while getting nothing for the Canadian people. 

I haven't forgotten that he was in Tuscany on a "personal" trip when the 50% tariff deadline was hanging over the country. He has the worst Question Period attendance of any modern prime minister with missing roughly three-quarters of them, including dozens of days he was already in Ottawa. And during Question Periods, I've seen him leave more than once. 

Parliament sits less, committees get stacked, and when a trade war he himself called a ‘war’ is underway he will not recall the House. Instead he'll to Strasbourg to address the European Parliament.

We found out about the first Canada-China military coordination talks in eight years from Beijing, not from our own government. But China's. That is the opposite of transparency.

Carney has not been an improvement on Trudeau. He is an unelected banker with more conflicts than most people will ever see, who treats Parliament as optional and treats Canadians as spectators. Electing him was the wrong choice. Accepting whatever deal Washington puts down is not the only alternative to this. Doing the actual job of a prime minister bye showing up, telling the public the truth, and facing the House, would have been the start.

Trump is a businessman running America First. That will not be gentle for us. He will tax our goods and pull plants home because that is what his job is. That was Ottawa.
Twelve years of volume as growth. Transfers that made a poverty line look kinder while the middle sat in the notch — too rich for the program, too poor for the break, first for the invoice. Public payrolls that never missed a deposit. Shops that did. GDP that can rise on a stage while GDP per person slips. Kids in the basement. Parents waiting for a doctor. A generation that no longer believes it will do better than we did.
Now they want a fight with the only customer that takes most of what we sell, and they want you to cheer the speech. Whatever it takes. They’re mean. We walked. Midnight levy. Strasbourg on the calendar. The rejected text is not on the table. The exit file is not on the table.
Sovereignty is not a video. Sovereignty is whether your country still works on Friday.
I lived the last version. Trudeau Senior. The NEP. It did not start with the layoff. It started with a government that could not see the kitchen table. Then the keys. Then the diner. Then the hotel. Then towns that felt like Main Street was in receivership. When doors shutter, the middle class eats it first. We do not have a parachute this time. They already spent the room to move.
So here is the forest.
The enemy picture they sold you is a man in Washington.
The bill you pay was written here — policy, ideology, a room that grocery-shops from a briefing note.
Enough.
Not enough as a hashtag. Enough as a demand. GDP per person, not GDP for the camera. Who came in on the permit the cities could not house. What share of the litre is still tax. The offer they walked away from. A pipe that is steel, not paper. A government that looks at the table before it looks at the globe.
Hold the table.
Not the slogan.
Not the monster they built so you would not notice who put the keys on the counter.

text:
FROM SPECTATOR TO OFFERING: At Mass, Your Body Prays Too

We enter Mass thinking that prayer is merely a matter of thought or feeling. We are mistaken. God did not redeem only your soul; He redeemed your body on the Cross to make it an instrument of worship. You do not go to Mass merely to watch something; you go to offer your whole self.

1. Your body is not your own; it is a temple, bought at the price of Blood.
Modernity claims the body is nothing more than biology. The Catholic faith declares it sacred.
"Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you...? You have been purchased at a great price. Therefore, glorify God with your body." (1 Cor 6:19-20)

"We await the redemption of our bodies." (Rom 8:23)
Paragraph 364 of the *Catechism of the Catholic Church* teaches that the human body shares in the dignity of being made in God's image, and paragraph 1004 reminds us that we will be resurrected in our glorified bodies. If Christ intends to resurrect it, how could He not desire for it to worship Him now?

You do not merely bring your body to Mass; your body *goes* to Mass to encounter its Redeemer.

2. True love requires kneeling: your gestures are not theater; they are theology.
God created us with gestures because love cannot remain confined to the mind. In the liturgy, every posture is a prayer that the Church has safeguarded for centuries (SC 33).

Standing: The posture of the risen one—of the person who is ready and attentive. This is how we listen to the Gospel.
Kneeling: The radical humility of the creature before its Creator. Jesus Himself prayed on His knees (Lk 22:41). "At the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven and on earth and under the earth" (Phil 2:10). Bowing and prostrating: "Come, let us bow down and worship, kneeling before the Lord our Maker" (Ps 95:6). We acknowledge our littleness.
Striking the breast and making the Sign of the Cross: You confess with your flesh that you are a sinner and that you have been saved. "My soul thirsts for you; my flesh yearns for you" (Ps 63:2).

When you do not kneel, stand only halfway, or sit as if at a show, your soul learns laziness. When you worship with your body, your soul learns reverence.

3. What you do outwardly transforms what is within.
The Church did not invent empty gestures. It gave us tangible signs so that the visible might lead us to the invisible (CCC 1146). Your body educates your soul.
"I urge you to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God—this is your spiritual worship." (Rom 12:1)
That is the miracle of the Mass: you do not merely contemplate Christ’s Sacrifice; you unite yourself to it. If your body is distracted, your offering is half-hearted. If your body is composed, attentive, and reverent, your soul is better disposed to receive Christ in the Eucharist.

Arrive five minutes early and offer your body: "Lord, today I worship You with all that I am."
Live out each posture consciously, not out of routine. When you kneel during the Consecration, do so slowly, knowing that Heaven is touching earth.
Let your posture preach. A young person kneeling with love in a distracted church evangelizes more than a thousand words.

The "I Am" Connection is inherently woven into the fabric of human speech. Whenever a person speaks about themselves—such as saying "I am [name]"—they invoke the "I am" of God first. 
The Constant Presence: Even in moments of perceived isolation or failure (e.g., saying "I am alone" or "I am sinful"), the user is still articulating the name of God. This serves as a reminder that God’s presence is never absent; He joins Himself to our experiences, ensuring we are never truly alone. 
His presence is constant, joining Himself to our personal experiences, ensuring we are never truly separated from Him. 
The Source of Existence: Because God is the ultimate "I Am," every individual’s existence is tied to His, because we must say His name to speak of our own identity, it signifies that we were created to live from God, not just for Him. 
Putting God First: The mystery suggests that we find the true purpose and fulfillment of our lives only when we acknowledge God as the primary reality. His love is shown to be the very foundation of our being, as our lives move and exist only because He is. 
✨️💖 The "Bridegroom" mystery illustrates that salvation is an act of God initiating a relationship with humanity, rather than humans needing to earn their way to Him. 
God is the Bridegroom: Just as the groom had to journey to his bride regardless of her circumstances, God made the ultimate journey from heaven to earth 2,000 years ago to reach humanity. 
Initiative of Grace: Humans cannot bridge the gap to reach God on their own; instead, He is the one who comes to us, regardless of the "mess" or the state of our lives, to propose a covenant relationship. 
Our Response: Salvation is presented as an invitation. Our role is simply to "open up" the door of our lives to Him and accept His offer by saying "I do". 
This mystery underscores that we do not need to reach a standard of perfection to be worthy of God; rather, He comes to where we are to invite us into His life. 
✨️💖 The East-West continuum A Symbol of Infinite Distance: While the North-South axis on Earth is finite because it is defined by two poles, an East-West axis is infinite because there are no "East" or "West" poles. You can travel in one direction forever without ever reaching an end. 
God's Atonement: This geophysics serves as a shadow of our salvation in Messiah. Just as there is no end to the East or West, God has removed our sins an infinite distance away, making them impossible to find again. 
Temple Layout: Historically, the Temple of Jerusalem was designed according to this continuum. The altar of sacrifice was in the East, and the Holy of Holies was in the West. During the Day of Atonement, the high priest moved between these points to perform the rituals of cleansing, visually acting out the removal of sins on this infinite axis. 
The Unending Love of God: The Psalmist writes that God has removed our transgressions from us as far as the East is from the West. This reveals that God's love and mercy are not limited; they are beyond exhaustion, keeping going forever with no boundaries.

Living from Him: This mystery teaches that one does not just live to God, but must learn to live from Him. By acknowledging that our own "I am" flows from His "I Am," we find the secret to a life anchored in His eternal presence.

text:
"Reportedly"? 

From Gemini:

The viral post is mostly false and severely distorts the findings of the Haaretz investigation. 

While parts of the dialogue reflect reporting from a book published in Haaretz, the post strips away critical context, fabricates the claim that Hamas asked for "nothing," and draws an unsupported conclusion about Antony Blinken.  

What the Haaretz Report Actually Details:

The claims originate from an excerpt published by Haaretz from an investigative book (Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment by journalists Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval):  

The Qatari Outreach: 

In the chaotic hours immediately following October 7, Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani pressured Hamas leadership (threatening them with expulsion from Doha) to release civilian captives. Qatar did contact both Israel (Mossad chief David Barnea) and U.S. Secretary of State Antony Blinken to explore whether a rapid release could be brokered.  

Israel's Initial Refusal:

Barnea reportedly responded: "If they want to release the civilians, let them release them. We are not prepared to speak with Hamas." 

At the time, Israeli security officials argued that Hamas was attempting to impose non-starters (like halting Israeli military retaliation and changing prayer access at the Temple Mount), while Qatari officials maintained the initial civilian release proposal carried no major preconditions.  

Blinken’s Dialogue: 

When Al Thani spoke with Blinken, urging immediate action, Blinken asked to wait until he arrived in the region: "Right now, the situation is complex. Israel is still under attack, and there's no one to talk to. 

We will wait three days [until I meet with Netanyahu personally]."  

Where the Post Distorts the Facts

"Hamas offered to return all civilians for nothing":

This is misleading. First, Hamas was holding hostages while actively killing over a thousand people inside southern Israel. 

Second, accounts differ sharply: Israeli officials reported that Hamas was already seeking a total halt to incoming IDF operations. 

Third, Hamas's definition of "civilian" excluded any military-age Israeli men (whom they categorized as reservists or combatants).  

"Blinken told Qatar he didn't want to hear it":

False. Blinken did not reject diplomacy; he noted the practical impossibility of opening indirect negotiations while active gunbattles were still taking place across southern Israeli towns and kibbutzim.  

"Blinken wanted war instead of freeing hostages": 

A gross mischaracterization. 
The same report confirms that Blinken flew to Tel Aviv on October 12, pressed Netanyahu directly on opening hostage channels, flew to Doha on October 13 to coordinate with Al Thani, and texted Qatar on October 14 confirming: "Netanyahu is ready for you to mediate. The Mossad director will arrive soon."  

Blinken and the U.S. administration were actively building the very mediation channel through Qatar that ultimately secured the November 2023 temporary ceasefire and the release of over 100 hostages. 

The claim that Blinken refused the offer because he "wanted war" inverts the diplomatic timeline documented in the report.

The consensus spent all year debating entry points while ignoring the only decision that mattered: asset class selection.

Look at the tape across 12 asset classes through September 8:

• Commodities: +38.9% 
• Emerging Markets: +26.5% 
• U.S. Small Caps: +20.5% 
• U.S. Large Caps: +13.0% 
• Cash: +2.4% 
• Gold: +0.9% 
• TIPS: +0.8% 
• Core U.S. Bonds: -0.3% 
• Bitcoin: -10.6%

A 49.5 point spread from top to bottom in eight months.

How a macro allocator reads this board:

1.) Traditional Hedges Broke: Cash beat Gold, TIPS, and Core Bonds. Long-duration paper didn't protect you from inflation or term premium expansion. Cash was the only defensive asset that preserved nominal capital.

2.) The Small Cap Divergence: U.S. small caps are beating large caps by 7.5 percentage points. Same country, same currency. The rally is no longer concentrated in five mega-cap tech balance sheets.

3.) The Physical Tape Rules: With crude crossing $100 on Middle Eastern supply bottlenecks, physical assets are punishing paper promises.

Diversification isn't owning 30 stocks with the same beta. It’s holding balance sheets and assets that answer to fundamentally different macro plumbing.

This is the year the physical tape got paid.

text:
Hashem Al-Ghaili

Minneapolis converted a massive warehouse into an indoor neighborhood of 100 houses for the homeless.
Avivo Village, a first-of-its-kind indoor community, has transformed a 48,000-square-foot warehouse into a safe haven containing 100 private, lockable tiny homes for unhoused peoples.

Unlike traditional congregate shelters that offer only temporary mats on a shared floor, this low-barrier, trauma-informed shelter-within-a-shelter model provides residents with their own heated spaces, electricity, and the freedom to stay with their pets.
By prioritizing dignity and security, the village offers a safe starting point for individuals who typically avoid standard shelter environments due to safety concerns.

The impact of this innovative model extends far beyond providing a warm roof. Operating under a harm-reduction philosophy, Avivo Village serves as a comprehensive care hub, offering residents immediate on-site access to mental health therapy, substance use disorder treatment, and dedicated case managers. The results speak volumes: since its inception in December 2020, the village has served over 870 individuals, successfully transitioned nearly 340 people into permanent, stable housing, and reversed over 260 on-site overdoses.

As cities across the United States grapple with growing housing crises, this warehouse-to-village conversion offers a scalable, compassionate blueprint for turning empty urban infrastructure into lifesaving community hubs.
source: Minnesota Department of Human Services. (2026). Avivo Village: Indoor tiny home shelter in Minneapolis

text:
Victor Davis Hanson, a military classicist, historian, and fellow at the Hoover Institution, offered some insight into why Tucker Carlson, Marjorie Taylor Greene, and others, who initially appeared to be allies of the MAGA movement, so quickly became saboteurs.

According to Hanson, it may simply be that when these commentators and politicians spoke with President Trump, they believed themselves capable of guiding the MAGA movement more broadly. In other words, like most people who get a taste for power, they believed they could single-handedly commandeer the movement for their own ends. When the president made clear that wasn’t going to happen, they showed their true colors.

“I think they felt that because they had been very intimate with [Trump] — in the sense that they had been at Mar-a-Lago, or they were on Air Force One — that they insidiously began to think that they could tell him things, and they forgot that he is the president of the United States, and that they represent maybe one-one thousandth of the people he contacts,” Hanson told Miranda Divine of "Pod Force One."

“This is a man who’s talking to the most powerful people in the world, and we’re not that important, but [Greene and Carlson] felt — I don’t know how else to explain why Tucker said he called him and said, ‘Don’t do this with Iran,’ or ‘Don’t do this,’ or ‘Don’t do that,’” he added.

“Why would a president listen to somebody just because he was on Air Force One, and why would Tucker, who’s a very intelligent person, think that he had that entree to affect a policy that would change decades just because he had been on Air Force One or had known Trump?”

text:
Robert E. Lee was a great American and a great Virginian.

History classes are not teaching him that way today. Rabid crowds are pulling his statues down.

I saw that shift happen slowly then all at once living so many decades here in Virginia.

I am glad that I learned the truth of it as a kid.

Lee was offered and refused a command in the Union army by Lincoln’s staff.

As an honorable man he had no choice but to command the forces of Virginia. In his own words:

Robert E. Lee, letter to his sister Anne Marshall Lee, April 20, 1861:

“With all my devotion to the Union, I have not been able to make up my mind to raise my hand against my relatives, my children, my home.”

Robert E. Lee, letter to General Winfield Scott, April 20, 1861:

“Save in defense of my native State, I never desire again to draw my sword.”

I won’t even get into his tireless efforts of reunification after the war.

This was a man that was not going to fight against his family and friends in Virginia. He wasn’t going to stand by and watch them be destroyed by the Union army. 

Is there anything more that needs to be said?

What would you have done in his position?

Mark, you (and you aren’t alone here so I don’t think you are stupid or anything) are making the mistake that a lot of people are making, which is confusing “Can I imagine some other possible explanation” as being “reasonable doubt”. It isn’t. There has to be either evidence of an alternative explanation, or proof that the evidence presented is insufficient to convict. The alternative explanations you offer here (similar to what the defense offered) don’t have evidence behind them. We don’t have evidence that a “demonic voice told her to do it,” we just have her statement, for example. 

If we considered every statement from every criminal who denies responsibility due to some other reason as material evidence, no one would be in jail lol. 

So even though you are correct in that Massachusetts the burden of proof flips in an insanity case, sufficient evidence still demonstrates that she is guilty for the reasons I proposed.

text:
Republicans and "Socialism" since 1854:

The early GOP heavily used federal power, land grants, and protectionist policies to rapidly build the American industrial economy.

The Transcontinental Railroad (Pacific Railroad Acts of 1862 & 1864): The Lincoln administration provided massive federal land grants and low-interest government bonds to private corporations. This heavily subsidized the construction of the nation's rail network.

The Homestead Act of 1862: This landmark program subsidized western migration by granting 160 acres of public land virtually free to any citizen who agreed to settle and farm it.

Public Universities (Morrill Land-Grant Acts): The federal government granted millions of acres of public land to states. States then sold this land to subsidize and build public universities focused on agriculture and engineering (such as Penn State, Ohio State, and Purdue).

High Protective Tariffs: While technically a tax on foreign imports, the GOP's signature 19th-century policy acted as a massive indirect subsidy for domestic manufacturers, shielding American steel, textiles, and factories from foreign competition.

As the nation urbanized, Republican administrations focused federal funding on large-scale engineering, natural resource management, and national security infrastructure.

Western Water Infrastructure (National Reclamation Act of 1902): Championed by President Theodore Roosevelt, this program used federal funds from public land sales to build dams and irrigation systems, subsidizing commercial agriculture in the arid American West.

The Interstate Highway System (Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956): President Dwight D. Eisenhower championed the largest public works project in American history up to that point. The federal government funded 90% of interstate construction costs, providing a permanent subsidy to the automotive, shipping, and logistics industries.

Higher Education and STEM (National Defense Education Act of 1958): Spurred by the Soviet Union's launch of Sputnik, Eisenhower championed federal funding for low-interest student loans, graduate fellowships, and public school equipment to boost math, science, and foreign language education.

Faced with expanding Democratic social programs, Republicans began pioneering safety net programs that relied on private markets, tax expenditures, and individual choices rather than traditional government bureaucracies.

The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC): Originally devised by conservative economists like Milton Friedman as a "negative income tax," the EITC was signed into law under President Gerald Ford in 1975. It remains a major refundable tax subsidy for low- to moderate-income working individuals.

Medicare Part B (1965): During negotiations over the creation of Medicare, Republicans successfully designed and championed Part B, which created a government-subsidized, voluntary private physician insurance system rather than a single-payer model.

Enterprise Zones: Championed by figures like Jack Kemp in the 1980s, these programs offered heavy tax incentives and regulatory relief to corporations that agreed to invest and create jobs in economically distressed urban neighborhoods.

text:
Ole Miss

1986 — NCAA major-infractions case. Ole Miss football is placed on two years’ probation following numerous NCAA violations. This becomes important later because the NCAA eventually views subsequent cases as evidence of a recurring institutional problem. 

1994 — Ole Miss football gets hammered by the NCAA again.

The case involves major recruiting violations, improper inducements, extra benefits, ethical-conduct violations and institutional-control problems. Allegations included offers of cash and cars to recruits and a university representative entertaining recruits at a Memphis-area strip club where alcohol was provided. 

Head coach Billy Brewer is fired while the investigation is underway. Athletic director Warner Alford resigns. 

The penalties include:

Four years probation
Two-year bowl ban
No television appearances during the 1995 season
Recruiting restrictions
Scholarships cut dramatically, including only 13 initial scholarships in each of two recruiting classes
Ole Miss appeals portions of the punishment. 

1997 — While still on NCAA probation, Ole Miss reports another football recruiting violation.

Tommy Tuberville and an assistant visited junior-college prospects during a no-contact period. Ole Miss self-reports it and stops recruiting the players. 

Then there’s a relatively quiet period.

And then Hugh Freeze arrives.

2012 — Hugh Freeze takes over Ole Miss.

Ole Miss rapidly becomes a major recruiting force.

But behind that rise, violations are accumulating.

2010–15 — NCAA investigation eventually expands across multiple Ole Miss sports.

This becomes important because the eventual cases aren’t limited to football.

Women’s basketball staff members commit academic fraud to keep athletes eligible.

Track staff members commit recruiting violations and provide false or misleading information during the NCAA investigation. 

2016 — NCAA major-infractions decision involving women’s basketball and track.

The NCAA finds:

Academic fraud
Unethical conduct
False or misleading information
Failure to monitor
Failure to promote an atmosphere of compliance
And football is still being investigated separately. 

2016–17 — The Ole Miss football investigation explodes.

The NCAA ultimately finds that:

Six football staff members and 12 boosters participated in violations.

Prospects received approximately $37,000 in improper benefits, including:

Cash
Cars
Lodging
Transportation
Meals
Clothing
And it gets worse.

Two staff members helped arrange fraudulent standardized-test scores for three prospects. 

February 2017 — Ole Miss self-imposes a bowl ban.

The university announces it will keep the football team out of the 2017 postseason as the NCAA case continues.

July 2017 — Hugh Freeze resigns.

And strangely, the NCAA violations aren’t directly what finally brings him down.

Former Ole Miss coach Houston Nutt’s legal dispute with the university leads to examination of Freeze’s university cellphone records.

A call to a number associated with an escort service is discovered.

Ole Miss initially believes it could have been a misdial.

Administrators investigate further.

They discover what Chancellor Jeffrey Vitter describes as a:

“pattern of personal misconduct.”

Athletic director Ross Bjork says Ole Miss would have fired Freeze for cause had he not resigned. 

A subsequent review of phone records finds at least 12 calls to numbers associated with escort-service advertisements over approximately 33 months. 

Cont….

text:
Josh, I listened to your missive (rant!) and think you're on to something here. 

Let me say I agree humanities is wounded, but I think that's indicative of the movement overall of questioning post-secondary education, because: 

1) we have the 'educational loan industrial complex' which oversubscribed parents and schools into pushing kids into college who probably shouldn't (i.e., should go to trades, should take a year at community college to see if they really want to, should go to military, etc), and now kids and parents are pushing back (high schools not so much). Yes there's still a predominant mentality to go take out a huge student loan, but we now have some people questioning that, which is good. 
2) the woke illiberal take-over in most institutions was exposed during covid and post covid. You had schools (like Penn State) restricting speakers from coming on campus because of feelings or whatever. You had schools allowing pro-Palestinians block other students from entering buildings and classrooms, and bullying or assaulting Jewish or pro-Israel supporters. Can you imagine this? Protests and rallies are a key feature of learning and institutions but they can never be permitted to block free passage, never allowed to block buildings, never disrupt professors from holding their classes, and certainly never assault students who don't agree. 

I think parents are pushing back on those things. That's why college enrollment is declining (not just humanities). Thus it's logical to imagine that there will be adjustments: Some schools will fail altogether. Some schools will change their size. Some will change their majors. 

I'm an education purest: I think humanities is the building block of a civilized and virtuous society. We can't let those go. I think some of other majors are "job training." I think kids/students should be allowed to choose the path that makes sense for them; so I like Finance as a major, but I also like English as a major. 

There needs to be good pathways for kids that take English, or History, etc., as a major, because a Finance major can go out and get a decent paying job right after their undergrad, whereas an English or History major may have a hard time. 

I do think Education major should be considered for elimination. An Education "certificate" should be offered, but not majored in. School teachers in all grades should have a "real" degree, like English, History, Science, whatever. Even if they will teach multiple subjects in early grades... Those subjects are better foundation than someone with an "education" degree. Perhaps education as a field of study could be important, maybe a minor. But I digress. 

With my own children as examples, my youngest son just started his freshman year. Because he wants to be a lawyer, there is a logical pathway that benefits from a humanities degree. So he agreed to dual-major in Economics and History. He'll get a full History degree which I hope is structured similar to how you envisioned what an English degree should look like, and he'll get an Economics degree (which I argue is between a humanities degree and social science or business degree). He could fall back on Econ in the job market if he decides NOT to pursue law school. But getting grounded in History and Economics is one of the best foundations before going to law school (and you can argue so is English and Philosophy). 

Additionally he's take a minor and they ARE reading full books (he was assigned Plato five dialogues and St. Augustine Confessions right off the bat! I was very excited to hear this and so was my son -- that's right, I raised a right proper geek!)

I realize in my example most kids can't do two majors unless they come in with 30 credits or so. But the same approach applies: the pathway after undergrad sort of dictates what to major in. If you're going to the business world, probably a business degree. If you're going to medicine or law or education, probably humanities or science. 

My other two kids both did business. One earned a Finance degree from FSU (and now runs his own business), the other is a senior and she is pursuing a marketing degree (I'll leave school name off since she's still attending). 

Business majors were right for them, but humanities is right for my youngest. I think kids that should take humanities are the ones who read books growing up and score at the top of their class in reading level, and high SAT... 

Humanities doesn't have to die; it is wounded and I love your suggestion for an English major.

Have you considered reaching out to the Hamilton School at UF to see if your idea would fit their approach or if you are a good fit for them? They have a "great books and ideas" major which I place squarely as an existential humanities degree that is probably better than the typical big school english degree (just my opinion).

Dear members of the American press!

Steve Jobs once said, "If you can convince the press of your technology, and the press convinces us, we'll pay attention."

That's why I'm reaching out to you.

For years, the development of personal devices has been driven by advances in smartphones, tablets, and virtual reality technologies. However, all of these solutions still require people to adapt to the device.
