text:
1. I’m putting this out there knowing I might get some hate for it.
   As of today, Thursday, June 11:

2. SKHY → Don’t buy now.

3. These are just my own views, so feel free to disagree or criticize me.
   Read through my feed carefully and you’ll start to get a feel for when to take profits too.

4. Rocket Lab was told by the U.S. Space Force to launch a satellite within 24 hours.

5. Rocket Lab did it in just 16 hours and 42 minutes. lol

6. They even approached a satellite that SpaceX had launched earlier and took pictures of it.

7. But on the day Rocket Lab announced the successful mission, its stock dropped 10%.

8. What the U.S. government bought from Rocket Lab wasn’t just a rocket, and Rocket Lab had already burned through almost all of the government funding. lol

9. What the Space Force had asked Rocket Lab to do was a military experiment involving satellites approaching and tracking other satellites.

10. SpaceX launched a satellite for True Anomaly back in May.

11. Rocket Lab, on the other hand, built the satellite itself, launched it, and handled its operation and maneuvering in space.

12. The contract had been signed two years earlier, so Rocket Lab built the satellite in advance and kept it ready.

13. The target orbit was provided along with the launch order in June.

14. So how much did the Space Force pay Rocket Lab for the preparation and the mission?

15. $32 million. 

16. That amount covered everything—from building the satellite to launching it and operating it once it was in orbit.

17. The satellite-to-satellite approach and imaging test had an 84-hour limit, but Rocket Lab completed it in 59 hours.

18. Rocket Lab wasn’t selling a single rocket launch. It was selling the ability to get the job done within the required time when called upon.

19. But if SpaceX already exists, why have another company do this?

20. Because the U.S. government wants to have another company it can call on when things get urgent.

21. Being in a hurry doesn’t mean you can sign a contract with just any company today and have a satellite launched tomorrow.

22. You need to test in advance whether a company can build the rocket, build the satellite, and actually execute the mission.

23. Even if it costs more, you develop and maintain that capability ahead of time.

24. The Space Force itself said that after this experiment, it now had two companies—Rocket Lab and True Anomaly—that it could turn to when needed.

25. But more than 10 years ago, NASA once tried to choose just one company.

26. The company that nearly got left out was SpaceX. lol

27. In 2014, NASA was selecting companies to transport astronauts to the International Space Station.

28. Boeing offered to do it for $4.2 billion, while SpaceX offered $2.6 billion.

29. SpaceX was $1.6 billion cheaper, but price barely even came up during the NASA meeting.

30. Boeing received the higher technical and management scores and was a company NASA was already familiar with after working together for years.

31. There were even comments that working with SpaceX would be a hassle. lol

32. When the meeting ended, the selection paperwork listed only Boeing.

33. But one person pushed back: NASA’s associate administrator responsible for human spaceflight.

34. His argument was simple: if something went wrong with the Boeing spacecraft, who would bring the astronauts home?

35. He argued that NASA should select both companies, even if it meant spending more on development.

36. When he couldn’t get the idea through in the meeting, he reportedly went to the office of the person with final decision-making authority almost every day.

37. He was even scolded for saying that choosing only one company was reckless.

38. In the end, NASA selected both Boeing and SpaceX.

39. The SpaceX that barely made it in as the second company back then is now considered a Tier-1 contractor in U.S. Space Force programs. lol

40. In April this year, the Space Force launched a program for satellites designed to track airborne targets and selected nine candidate companies.

41. SpaceX received the first order, worth $4.2 billion.

42. The mission is to build a military satellite network capable of tracking airborne targets through 2028.

43. Then the second order was awarded.

44. Rocket Lab received $400 million, and together with STR and one undisclosed company, the total came to $600 million.

45. A Space Force colonel explicitly said the second order was placed so they wouldn’t have to rely on the technology of just one company.

46. SpaceX got $4.2 billion, while roughly one-seventh of that amount was split among the other three companies.

47. It’s basically the same situation as NASA leaving SpaceX behind Boeing in 2014—except this time SpaceX is number one and Rocket Lab is number two. lol

48. Rocket Lab’s role is to provide satellites that track aircraft in space.

49. The satellites will track moving airborne targets and relay that information to the military.

50. That’s something reconnaissance aircraft handle today, but satellites can do the tracking in areas where sending a reconnaissance aircraft would be too dangerous.

51. The $400 million contract also includes options for additional satellites.

52. Rocket Lab will build the satellites, launch them on its own rockets, and operate them.

53. Only two companies can handle both the satellite and the launch: SpaceX and Rocket Lab.

54. Last December, Rocket Lab also won a contract for 18 military satellites designed to monitor and track missiles.

55. The base contract alone is worth $800 million, or more than ₩1 trillion.

56. Rocket Lab is responsible for everything from satellite design and manufacturing to operations.

57. But another company also won a separate satellite contract under the same program.

58. So is the business that company won simply revenue Rocket Lab missed out on?

59. No. Rocket Lab has multiple lines of business.

60. One is building and selling complete satellites.

61. The other is selling satellite components—solar panels, attitude sensors, reaction wheels, and so on.

62. Even satellites built by other companies can contain Rocket Lab components, such as its Starlight protective sensor.

63. It’s similar to Samsung selling Galaxy phones while also supplying memory chips to Apple.

64. The exact amounts sold to each customer haven’t been disclosed, but the company estimates the total opportunity, including component sales, at around $1 billion.

65. What about the rockets? Does Rocket Lab make more money launching rockets than it does selling satellites and components?

66. The rocket business isn’t actually the main business. lol

67. Satellite and component revenue is more than four times larger.

68. In Q2 this year, out of $230 million in total revenue, Space Systems—which sells satellites and components—generated $190 million, or about 80%.

69. Launch Services generated $45 million, or about 20%.

70. Launching rockets is basically the business of putting other people’s satellites into orbit on Electron.

71. The company is called Rocket Lab, but only about $2 out of every $10 in revenue comes from launching rockets. lol

72. So does that mean it’s okay if development of the new rocket takes a little longer?

73. No. There are two reasons.

74. First, the Electron that launched in 16 hours and 42 minutes is a small rocket capable of carrying around 300 kg.

75. The Space Force’s satellite network requires multiple satellites to be launched, so it needs the 13-ton Neutron to handle the job.

76. Second, why not just launch them on a SpaceX rocket?

77. Because then there would be no point in having a second company the Space Force can call on when it needs something urgently.

78. The Space Force itself said the second order was placed specifically to avoid relying on a single company’s technology.

79. But Neutron has never reached space yet.

80. In January this year, a Neutron tank ruptured during a tank pressure test.

81. Rocket Lab is currently assembling and testing its first flight vehicle.

82. The company’s goal is to send it to the launch site in Q4 this year.

83. That means sending it to the launch site—not actually launching it.

84. The company’s filings say the window to launch within this year is getting tighter and tighter.

85. Rocket Lab received the orders first, but the rocket needed to fulfill those orders is still being built.

86. And even though it has a contract for 18 satellites, that doesn’t mean they’ll all be delivered immediately.

87. The final satellite is scheduled to be delivered in 2029.

88. Until then, Rocket Lab has to hire people, buy components, and manufacture everything. If the schedule slips, costs go up.

89. Even with a large contract, how much money the company actually makes depends on how much it spends and when it delivers.

90. So does Rocket Lab have cash left over right now?

91. No.

92. Its operating loss in Q2 was $58 million.

93. For every $10 of revenue, it costs more than $6 to produce what it sells, leaving about $3.60.

94. But R&D costs another $3.50.

95. In other words, R&D eats up almost all of the gross profit.

96. On top of that, another $2.50 goes toward employees and running the company.

97. So for every $10 in revenue, Rocket Lab spends $12.50, resulting in a $2.50 loss.

98. Not all of that is because of Neutron, but while R&D spending remains this high, it’s difficult to generate a profit.

99. So how does Rocket Lab survive while losing money?

100. It survives on cash. As of the end of June, it had $2.4 billion in cash and almost no debt.

101. But that money wasn’t accumulated through profits. It came from selling stock.

102. Over the past year and a half, Rocket Lab has sold $2.7 billion worth of stock, and its share count increased by 25% in one year.

103. The company burns a little over $300 million a year.

104. So $2.4 billion gives it roughly seven years of runway, which is why it isn’t in immediate danger despite the losses.

105. But Rocket Lab has decided to use that cash for something else. lol

106. It announced plans to acquire satellite communications company Iridium for $8 billion.

107. Iridium generates about $400 million in operating cash annually—more than Rocket Lab burns in a year.

108. Rocket Lab plans to pay for the acquisition with roughly half cash and half Rocket Lab stock.

109. Because it doesn’t have enough cash on hand, it plans to borrow $3.6 billion from banks and issue more stock.

110. Rocket Lab’s stock jumped 16% on the announcement.

111. The acquisition is targeted to close in mid-2027.

112. After that, Iridium’s profits and the interest expense from the acquisition debt will start flowing through Rocket Lab’s financial statements.

113. But what happens to the stock price?

114. Rocket Lab went from $25 in 2025 to $150 this year—a sixfold increase.

115. It’s now around $66, more than 50% below its high.

116. Its biggest one-day gain this year was May 8, when it jumped 34%—the day after earnings and news of additional Neutron bookings.

117. Its biggest drop came on the trading day after SpaceX received the first Space Force order for the airborne-target program.

118. It fell 15%.

119. It also dropped around 10% on SpaceX’s IPO day and on the day Rocket Lab announced the successful 16-hour-42-minute mission.

120. In August, the Space Force order triggered four days of gains, but the stock gave all of it back within a month.

121. It’s now trading below where it was before the Space Force order.

122. What drove the stock higher was the Neutron bookings and the Iridium acquisition announcement.

123. Ironically, successful mission announcements often sent the stock lower. lol

124. Rocket Lab’s market cap is $39.4 billion.

125. That valuation is almost entirely based on expectations for what the company will earn in the future.

126. Its market cap is about 51 times its trailing-12-month revenue.

127. So let’s work backward and calculate how much revenue Rocket Lab would need to justify its current market cap.

128. Three major defense companies have net margins around 8% and P/E ratios around 20x based on their most recent results.

129. The most expensive aerospace component companies have margins of roughly 16–21% and P/E ratios of 35–53x.

130. If you value Rocket Lab like a major defense contractor, it would need $25 billion in annual revenue.

131. Even using the most generous aerospace-component valuation, it would need $3.5 billion in revenue to justify the current market cap.

132. That’s about five times its current revenue.

133. Even including Iridium, Wall Street estimates for 2027 net income are still less than one-fifth of what would be required under that generous scenario.

134. So how much could Rocket Lab actually make if Neutron succeeds?

135. The company says the launch price will be $50–55 million per launch.

136. Current contracts include five launches for undisclosed customers, one dedicated Space Force launch, plus the airborne-target satellite program.

137. Even at 20 launches a year, that would generate only around $1 billion in revenue.

138. That’s just one-third of the $3.5 billion revenue figure under the generous valuation scenario.

139. At a 43% launch-services margin, that would leave roughly $450 million in gross profit.

140. Neutron alone isn’t what justifies the current market cap.

141. What’s priced into the current valuation is how many more satellite-network contracts Rocket Lab can win.

142. Now let’s look at the timeline.

143. Orders have been piling up for about two and a half years—from the $32 million Space Force contract in April 2024 to the $400 million airborne-target contract this August.

144. Backlog is around $3 billion.

145. The company has funded its cash runway by selling $2.7 billion worth of stock, while Neutron’s first launch is still no earlier than the end of this year.

146. The company has already stated the conditions for turning profitable.

147. Starting the quarter after Neutron’s first successful flight, it expects to become operating-profit positive before depreciation and amortization.

148. Then, 18–24 months after that, it expects to turn cash-flow positive.

149. So if Neutron succeeds in early 2027, Rocket Lab could become profitable around mid-2027, with actual cash generation not arriving until late 2028 or 2029.

150. The Iridium acquisition is expected to close in mid-2027, while the 18 satellites are scheduled to be fully delivered by 2029.

151. Analysts expect Rocket Lab alone to remain loss-making in 2027, but potentially become profitable when Iridium is included.

152. So does winning government contracts automatically mean shareholders will make money?

153. The government needs a second company besides SpaceX to call on when things get urgent, so it spends money to develop that capability in advance.

154. Rocket Lab has demonstrated that it can build, launch, and operate satellites, and it also sells components to competing satellite manufacturers.

155. But Neutron, which is supposed to launch the Space Force’s satellite network, hasn’t even flown yet.

156. The money Rocket Lab makes from selling products is being consumed by R&D.

157. Its cash runway was built through stock sales, and it plans to strengthen its earnings by acquiring Iridium.

158. The stock price is already ahead of the company’s current fundamentals.

159. Neutron’s success is already priced in.

160. For the current market cap to make sense, Rocket Lab needs to win several more satellite-network contracts.

161. When the stock jumps on a contract announcement, investors are looking at the headline contract value.

162. How much money Rocket Lab actually keeps is determined after the work is completed and the satellites are delivered.

163. A company that the government needs and a company that makes money for its shareholders are two different things.

164. There are four things I’m watching now.

165. First, whether Neutron actually makes it to the launch site in Q4.

166. Second, whether its first launch successfully reaches orbit.

167. Third, whether Rocket Lab wins the next Space Force airborne-target order.

168. The backlog needs to keep growing beyond $3 billion for the current market-cap calculation to start making more sense.

169. Fourth, whether Q3 revenue exceeds R&D spending.

170. And finally, whether the Iridium acquisition closes in mid-2027 and how Rocket Lab plans to repay the $3.6 billion bridge loan.

171. Of these, the Neutron news will come first.

text:
A veteran hockey star just voluntarily threw away four million dollars cash to get fired, and his team is actually celebrating.

The Anaheim Ducks placed 35-year-old forward Chris Kreider on unconditional waivers for contract termination. That move wipes his $6.5 million cap hit off their books completely.

Why would a star walk away from a guaranteed $4,000,000 salary?

Because Kreider wanted out, and Anaheim needed cash fast. The Ducks were trapped after matching a huge offer sheet for Leo Carlsson. That left them with under $9 million in cap space while trying to re-sign Cutter Gauthier, who scored 41 goals last season.

Here is the obscure detail. Kreider did not just agree to rip up his deal. He quietly warned the entire league that if a team outside his preferred East Coast destination claims him on waivers, he simply will not report. He literally forfeited $4 million just to pick his own zip code.

Leo Carlsson even admitted Kreider gave him a high five for getting paid right before packing his bags. Anaheim gets cap space to lock down Gauthier, and Kreider gets his freedom.

When resources get tight, personal leverage is the only currency that matters.

Taking a short-term pay cut is sometimes the fastest way to buy total freedom.

Did Kreider save the Ducks from a cap nightmare, or did Anaheim push out a veteran leader to fix their own mistake?
